I started from my sleep with horror; a cold dew covered my forehead, my teeth chattered, and every limb became convulsed; when, by the dim and yellow light of the moon, as it forced its way through the window shutters, I beheld the being whom I had created. He held up the curtain of the bed; and his eyes, if eyes they may be called, were fixed on me. His jaws opened, and he muttered some inarticulate sounds, while a grin wrinkled his cheeks. One hand was stretched out towards me.

In the account which fear might once have dictated, I should have fled from that hand as from the grasp of a corpse returned to execute some unholy office. Even now I cannot recall the instant without a renewed sense of the tumult which possessed me. My first impulse was to spring from the bed, to gain the door, to descend into the courtyard and there await the morning among the rain and stones. My foot was already upon the floor. Yet the sound he made arrested me. It possessed no menace that I could distinguish. It rose and fell, broken, uncertain, like the attempt of an infant to shape a want for which no language had yet been given him. His fingers trembled in the cold air. His immense frame was bent, as though the effort of standing had already wearied limbs so newly called into action, and his wet hair hung about a countenance which my own hands had fashioned and which I now surveyed with a loathing I am ashamed to have felt so wholly.

Shame, perhaps, stayed me when reason would have counselled flight. I had pursued the secret of life through charnel-houses and dissecting rooms; I had deprived myself of rest, of health, of every domestic affection, that this form might breathe. Now that it breathed, I beheld only the failure of my ambition, and wished the work unmade. Was this, then, the boasted triumph of my knowledge, that I should animate a living being and abandon him in the first hour of his sensations to cold and terror?

"Do not fear," I said, though the words were addressed almost as much to myself as to him.

He turned his head at my voice. The sound that issued from his throat became softer, almost questioning. His hand remained extended. I forced myself to rise. My knees shook beneath me, and the room appeared to reel, for the dream from which I had awakened still pressed upon my imagination with its dreadful transformation of Elizabeth into the corpse of my mother. The creature watched my approach without advancing. When I came within reach, I took his hand.

It was cold, and so vast that my fingers could not close around it. The skin, which I had selected and joined with such minute labour, was rough at the knuckles and damp from the night air. He started at the contact, then looked down at our joined hands with an attention so profound that my terror began, against my will, to mingle with wonder. His fingers closed very slowly, lest, as I afterwards understood, he should hurt me. The pressure nevertheless made me wince. He perceived it, uttered a low cry, and at once released me, drawing back towards the wall with a countenance of confusion and distress.

"No," I said, and held out my hand again. "Gently. So."

He obeyed. This time his grasp was cautious. I led him from the bedside into the adjoining room, where the remains of my candle guttered above the instruments of my fatal work. The lifeless materials I had not yet removed lay covered by a sheet; at the sight of them he uttered another sound and pressed closer to me, his other hand catching at my sleeve. I drew the sheet more completely over what lay beneath and placed him upon a stool near the small stove, though the fire had long since sunk into ash.

***

I raked together the embers and laid upon them the few sticks that remained in the box beside the hearth. My hands, accustomed for months to the knife and the wire, now shook so violently that I twice let the tinder fall. The creature followed every motion. When the flame caught, he started and thrust his own hand towards the brightness. I seized his wrist before his fingers reached the coals.

"Fire," I said. "It burns."

He repeated no word, but looked from the flame to the place where I held him, and then, with a caution touching in so gigantic a frame, extended one finger nearer and withdrew it from the heat. A sound escaped him which might have been wonder. I fetched the blanket from my bed and threw it about his shoulders. It scarcely covered him. I added my travelling cloak, fastening it at his throat, for his nakedness increased both my horror and my remorse. He drew the folds together with his great hands and shivered beneath them, his teeth sounding faintly as the warmth began to reach him.

The apartment, in the grey approach of dawn, presented a spectacle of ruinous disorder: books and papers scattered upon the floor, jars and instruments crowded upon the table, the bed disordered by my brief and dreadful sleep, and in the midst of all, seated before a reviving fire, the being whose existence had been the sole object of my labours. Rain continued to patter against the panes. The church clock struck six. I became aware, with a pang that recalled me to the living world, that my clothes were damp where I had lain in them and that I had eaten nothing since the preceding afternoon.

In the small cupboard I found bread left by the servant, a piece of cheese wrapped in cloth, and a bottle in which some wine remained. I poured water from the ewer into a cup and set it before him. He looked at it without comprehension. I lifted my own cup, drank, and then offered his again. He imitated me clumsily, spilling much down his chin, and at the first swallow coughed and clutched the table. I tore the bread into pieces and ate one slowly. He did the same, examining the crust, pressing it between finger and thumb, and conveying it at last to his mouth with a gravity that would have moved me to laughter had my soul not been weighed down by a responsibility too vast for mirth.

"Bread," I said, touching the loaf. "Water." I laid my palm upon the cup. "Fire." I pointed to the stove. His lips moved. From them came a rough and imperfect sound, nearer to the last word than to the others. I repeated it, and he tried again, watching the motion of my mouth as a child watches the face of its instructor. When some resemblance rewarded him, his eyes brightened, and he struck his breast lightly with his open hand, as if demanding what name belonged to the being who had spoken.

I hesitated. What was he? The work of my hands, yet no work of wood or iron that could be laid aside when its maker tired of it. He breathed, he suffered cold, he learned. I placed my hand upon my own breast. "Victor," I said. Then I pointed towards him and remained silent.

He waited. His brow contracted. He touched himself and produced an interrogative murmur, looking at me with an eagerness that reproached my silence more sharply than any accusation. I had bestowed life without considering that life would require a place among living things. I shook my head, unable to supply what nature and society alike had denied him.

"Eat," I said at last, ashamed of my evasion, and pushed the bread nearer. He obeyed, though his gaze returned repeatedly to my face.

He comprehended that I wished him concealed, for he glanced towards the lock and then towards me, and a change passed over his countenance which I understood too well. He had learned already that his presence must be hidden.

I spent the morning in a state divided between sickness and an occupation so new that it continually recalled me from despair. I showed him the objects nearest to his wants and named them until the repetition wearied my own tongue. Hand. Coat. Door. Cup. He acquired sounds slowly, often confusing them, yet his memory retained what his articulation could not immediately reproduce. When I named the fire, he looked towards the stove with a mixture of attraction and dread whose existence I must record, although I still shrank from the lineaments in which it was expressed. When I named my own hand, he took it with the caution I had taught him and compared its size with his, turning both towards the light.

He would learn to compare himself with other men. He would demand from me an account of the solitude into which I had cast him, and what answer could I render that would not cover me with shame?

Towards noon I heard voices upon the stairs and hastily shut him into the workshop. In Ingolstadt I was known as a solitary student; visitors seldom sought me. Still, every footfall now suggested discovery, and every discovery some judgment upon the gigantic inhabitant concealed behind that door.

When I returned to him, he was standing close to the partition, his head inclined, listening. He pointed to the place where the woman's voice had sounded, then to himself, and shook his head slowly. I could not misunderstand him. He wished to know why he must not be seen.

I placed a chair before him and sat down opposite. "Men would fear you," I said, speaking slowly and accompanying the words with such gestures as I could devise. "They do not know you."

His lips laboured. "Victor," he said distinctly, and then touched his own breast.

I enjoined him by signs to remain upon the straw, placed bread and water within his reach, and locked the workshop door. The key felt heavier in my pocket than iron should feel. Near the inn at which the diligences stopped, I paused without knowing why, my eyes fixed upon a coach approaching from the other end of the street. As it drew nearer I observed that it was the Swiss diligence. It stopped where I stood, the door was opened, and Henry Clerval sprang out before the horses had wholly settled.

"My dear Frankenstein," he exclaimed, "how glad I am to see you! How fortunate that you should be here at the very moment of my alighting!"

His voice, his countenance, the familiar affection of his address, recalled my father, Elizabeth, and all those scenes of home so dear to my recollection. I grasped his hand and for one moment forgot the locked room behind me. Calm and serene joy, the first I had known for many months, rose within me; then the memory of what I concealed rendered that joy almost an act of treachery. What welcome could I offer him? What apartment could I shew him without falsehood?

Clerval continued talking of our mutual friends and of his good fortune in being permitted to come to Ingolstadt. "You may easily believe," said he, "how great was the difficulty to persuade my father that all necessary knowledge was not comprised in the noble art of book-keeping; and, indeed, I believe I left him incredulous to the last. But his affection for me at length overcame his dislike of learning, and he has permitted me to undertake a voyage of discovery to the land of knowledge."

"Tell me," I said, with an eagerness I strove to make natural, "how you left my father, my brothers, and Elizabeth."

"Very well, and very happy, only a little uneasy that they hear from you so seldom. By the by, I mean to lecture you a little upon their account myself." He stopped short and gazed full in my face. "But, my dear Frankenstein, I did not before remark how very ill you appear; so thin and pale; you look as if you had been watching for several nights."

The words, innocent in themselves, seemed to summon a sound from the distant apartment. I glanced involuntarily towards the college. Henry observed the direction of my eyes.

"It is ended," I said, "and begun. Henry, walk with me a little before we go up. The rain has left the air raw, yet I have need of it."

He took my arm, as he had done in happier days at Geneva, and allowed me to lead him once around the square while I asked after every member of my family. His answers gave me a pleasure embittered by the reflection that I could not share with him the cause of my silence. When at last we turned towards my lodgings, my pace slackened. I, who had crossed Europe in pursuit of a secret, dreaded the ascent of a familiar staircase.

I entreated Henry to wait a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs while I prepared my room for his reception. He laughed and accused me of German habits of seclusion, but consented. His head was raised, his lips parted, and in his whole attitude there was an attention so eager that I perceived he had distinguished Henry's tones from those of the servant.

I put my finger to my lips. He imitated the gesture gravely. I brought him a second blanket and was turning away when the unevenness of the floor betrayed me; a glass vessel fell from the table and broke with a sharp sound upon the boards. The creature started and knocked against the partition. From the staircase Henry called my name.

"Victor? Are you hurt?"

I heard his step upon the stair. Terror rendered me incapable of invention. I might have called out some explanation, might have met him at the door and invented illness or disorder, yet the habit of secrecy, already so fatal to me, closed my throat. The handle turned. Henry entered, carrying his travelling bag, and stopped upon the threshold.

The creature rose. In rising, his head approached the low beam, and the blanket slipped from one shoulder. Henry's bag fell from his hand. I saw the colour abandon his face, but he neither screamed nor fled. His eyes travelled from the immense limbs to the hands that had learned, only that morning, to close gently around mine, and thence to me.

"Victor," he said, in a voice scarcely audible, "what is this?"

The creature looked at Henry and then, seeking instruction, at me. "Victor," he pronounced, clearly enough.

Henry started more violently at the word than at the sight itself. "Good God, it speaks."

"He speaks," I said. "Henry, do not approach suddenly. He has done no harm. He is cold, and he has eaten bread from my hand, and if you raise your voice he will think—" I broke off, for I did not know what he would think, nor how much of our speech his quick intelligence already gathered from tone and gesture.

"No harm?" Henry whispered. "What have you done?"

Then, with the door shut behind us and the creature standing between the stove and the straw, I told him more than I had ever intended mortal ear should hear. I spoke in broken sentences: of my discovery, of the months spent among bones and corrupted matter, of the spark imparted on that dreary November night, and of the hand extended towards my bed. Henry listened without interruption, though his gaze often left my face for the silent figure beside us. When I had finished, he sank into a chair and covered his eyes.

"You should have written to your father," he said at length. "You should have written to me."

"Would you have believed me?"

"I believe my eyes," he replied, "and they accuse you more than disbelief could have done. You have kept this being locked among your instruments as if he were another instrument."

The creature, hearing the altered tone, uttered a low sound and drew nearer to me. Henry rose at once, but mastered himself and remained still. Slowly, and with many pauses, he held out his hand.

"Henry," I said, pointing to my friend. "Henry."

The creature looked at the offered hand. He glanced at me for permission, and, receiving it, extended his own with the same painful caution he had used before. Henry endured the touch, though I saw his fingers tremble. "Henry," the creature repeated imperfectly.

My friend withdrew his hand and turned to me with eyes full of horror and compassion. "We must get him proper clothing," he said. "And food. And no servant must come up unannounced. Victor, what do you mean to do with him?"

I had no answer. The question, spoken aloud by another, revealed the extent of my presumption. I had considered animation; I had not considered life.

***

Night closed over Ingolstadt with renewed rain. Henry, whose journey had fitted him for sleep, nevertheless refused to seek lodgings elsewhere until he had seen me eat and the creature supplied with broth purchased from an inn below. We spoke in low voices of practical necessities: a tailor who might be trusted with measurements too extraordinary to be explained, money for food, the removal of the remains still hidden beneath their sheet, and the necessity of preventing my landlord from entering the workshop. Each arrangement appeared possible for a day, and impossible for the life that must follow. Henry's kindness, which sustained me, also made my former solitude more criminal in my sight. He asked few questions concerning the principle by which life had been conferred, and I, cowardly even in confession, withheld the particulars.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we shall think more clearly. Tonight let him sleep."

We left the creature upon the straw, wrapped in blankets and my cloak, with a candle placed beyond his reach. Before the door closed, he lifted his head and pronounced my name, then Henry's, as if assuring himself that the sounds and the persons attached to them would remain. I lay down in my own bed exhausted, yet sleep, when it came, was broken by the recollection of his hand in mine.

I woke in darkness. The candle in the workshop had been extinguished, and moonlight entered through my shutters in narrow bars. He stood beside the bed, holding up the curtain as he had done on the first night. My heart beat violently, yet I did not cry out. He had come without noise, although the door between our rooms had been fastened; looking beyond him, I saw that he had lifted the latch with a delicacy I had not taught him.

He pointed to himself, then to me. "Victor," he said. His finger returned to his own breast. The word he sought was not my name, nor Henry's, nor any of the simple terms with which I had furnished him. He tried to shape it, failed, and struck his breast once, not in anger, but in a kind of desolate insistence. Then he took my hand, laid it against his face, and looked at me.

I understood the question before he found the sounds to ask it.

"Victor," he said again, and his great fingers closed cautiously around mine. "What— I?"

"It is ended," I said, "and begun. Henry, walk with me a little before we go up. The rain has left the air raw, yet I have need of it."

He took my arm, as he had done in happier days at Geneva, and allowed me to lead him once around the square while I asked after every member of my family. His answers gave me a pleasure embittered by the reflection that I could not share with him the cause of my silence. When at last we turned towards my lodgings, my pace slackened. I, who had crossed Europe in pursuit of a secret, dreaded the ascent of a familiar staircase.

***

I entreated Henry to wait a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs while I prepared my room for his reception. He laughed and accused me of German habits of seclusion, but consented. I ascended alone, unlocked the workshop, and found the creature seated precisely where I had left him, the untouched bread upon his knee. He had heard our voices below. His head was raised, his lips parted, and in his whole attitude there was an attention so eager that I perceived he had distinguished Henry's tones from those of the servant.

I put my finger to my lips. He imitated the gesture gravely. I brought him a second blanket and was turning away when the unevenness of the floor betrayed me; a glass vessel fell from the table and broke with a sharp sound upon the boards. The creature started and knocked against the partition. From the staircase Henry called my name.

"Victor? Are you hurt?"

I heard his step upon the stair. Terror rendered me incapable of invention. I might have called out some explanation, might have met him at the door and invented illness or disorder, yet the habit of secrecy, already so fatal to me, closed my throat. The handle turned. Henry entered, carrying his travelling bag, and stopped upon the threshold.

The creature rose. In rising, his head approached the low beam, and the blanket slipped from one shoulder. Henry's bag fell from his hand. I saw the colour abandon his face, but he neither screamed nor fled. His eyes travelled from the immense limbs to the hands that had learned, only that morning, to close gently around mine, and thence to me.

"Victor," he said, in a voice scarcely audible, "what is this?"

The creature looked at Henry and then, seeking instruction, at me. "Victor," he pronounced, clearly enough.

Henry started more violently at the word than at the sight itself. "Good God, it speaks."

"He speaks," I said. "Henry, do not approach suddenly. He has done no harm. He is cold, and he has eaten bread from my hand, and if you raise your voice he will think—" I broke off, for I did not know what he would think, nor how much of our speech his quick intelligence already gathered from tone and gesture.

"No harm?" Henry whispered. "What have you done?"

Then, with the door shut behind us and the creature standing between the stove and the straw, I told him more than I had ever intended mortal ear should hear. I spoke in broken sentences: of my discovery, of the months spent among bones and corrupted matter, of the spark imparted on that dreary November night, and of the hand extended towards my bed. Henry listened without interruption, though his gaze often left my face for the silent figure beside us. When I had finished, he sank into a chair and covered his eyes.

"You should have written to your father," he said at length. "You should have written to me."

"Would you have believed me?"

"I believe my eyes," he replied, "and they accuse you more than disbelief could have done. You have kept this being locked among your instruments as if he were another instrument."

The creature, hearing the altered tone, uttered a low sound and drew nearer to me. Henry rose at once, but mastered himself and remained still. Slowly, and with many pauses, he held out his hand.

"Henry," I said, pointing to my friend. "Henry."

The creature looked at the offered hand. He glanced at me for permission, and, receiving it, extended his own with the same painful caution he had used before. Henry endured the touch, though I saw his fingers tremble. "Henry," the creature repeated imperfectly.

My friend withdrew his hand and turned to me with eyes full of horror and compassion. "We must get him proper clothing," he said. "And food. And no servant must come up unannounced. Victor, what do you mean to do with him?"

I had no answer. The question, spoken aloud by another, revealed the extent of my presumption. I had considered animation; I had not considered life.

***

Night closed over Ingolstadt with renewed rain. Henry, whose journey had fitted him for sleep, nevertheless refused to seek lodgings elsewhere until he had seen me eat and the creature supplied with broth purchased from an inn below. We spoke in low voices of practical necessities: a tailor who might be trusted with measurements too extraordinary to be explained, money for food, the removal of the remains still hidden beneath their sheet, and the necessity of preventing my landlord from entering the workshop. Each arrangement appeared possible for a day, and impossible for the life that must follow. Henry's kindness, which sustained me, also made my former solitude more criminal in my sight. He asked few questions concerning the principle by which life had been conferred, and I, cowardly even in confession, withheld the particulars.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we shall think more clearly. Tonight let him sleep."

We left the creature upon the straw, wrapped in blankets and my cloak, with a candle placed beyond his reach. Before the door closed, he lifted his head and pronounced my name, then Henry's, as if assuring himself that the sounds and the persons attached to them would remain. I lay down in my own bed exhausted, yet sleep, when it came, was broken by the recollection of his hand in mine.

I woke before dawn to a cold that had not been in the room when I slept. The door to the workshop stood open upon the gallery. I called my name for him, as he called it for me, and received no answer. Upon the straw lay the blanket folded with a clumsy exactness; my travelling cloak was gone, and with it the bread, the cup, and Henry's spare gloves from the table where he had laid them. Wet marks, too large for any human foot, crossed the boards from the window and back again, for he had found the stair door unfastened below and had gone out not as a thief drops from a height, but as a man walks from a house that will not own him.

Upon the table, held down by the knife with which I had cut his bread, was a sheet torn from my notebook. He must have watched the direction of my hand through all our lessons, and practised when the locked door left him alone with my labels and discarded pages; for there, in charcoal, stood letters copied and recopied until they held. *VICTOR* was plain. Beneath it, larger, as if the hand had pressed in anger or in grief, he had written — *WHAT I* — and under that, twice begun and twice broken off, no word at all.

Henry came barefoot from the chair where he had at last slept, and read it over my shoulder. "Victor," he said, "the gates will not yet be open." I was already at the window. The rain had ceased, and in the first grey light the wet roofs shone empty all the way to the white steeple; but on the road beyond the court, where the mud kept every passage, one line of immense footprints went steadily away from us, and did not turn back.

The rain had imprisoned us at Thonon, and I remember the hour with a distinctness which no subsequent years have effaced; for we had travelled thither, when I was thirteen years of age, for a party of pleasure to the baths, and the inclemency of the heavens confined our whole company within the narrow limits of the inn. The windows were blurred with incessant showers; the mountains, which upon a fair morning had lifted their sublime shapes beyond the lake, were now concealed by vapour; the travellers loitered in the passages, and my younger brother fretted for the open air. For myself, denied the sublime shapes of hill and water which were wont to excite my curiosity concerning their causes, I sought such amusement as a strange house affords, and wandered from the public room to a small parlour where a former guest had left some tattered volumes upon a shelf.

Among them lay the work of Cornelius Agrippa, heavy, browned by age, exhaling that odour of dust which belongs to neglected learning; I opened it, I confess, with the mere apathy of a boy who would beguile an idle forenoon, and was presently seized by a wonder altogether new. He promised, in a style of daring confidence, the dominion of spirits, the transmutation of metals, the prolongation of life beyond its appointed frailty; he related facts so marvellous, and reasoned upon them with such apparent earnestness, that a new light seemed to dawn upon my ardent mind. Here, I thought, was no mere catalogue of names, no timid dissection which confessed its ignorance; here was a master who had penetrated deeper, who beheld the elements around him not as a peasant beholds them for their practical uses, but as a sovereign who commands their hidden laws. Bounding with a joy which I could not contain, I clasped the volume to my breast and hastened along the creaking gallery to seek my father, who sat beside a window where the rain coursed down the panes.

Young Victor Frankenstein offers the Agrippa volume to Alphonse Frankenstein in the Thonon inn, and I can still see the posture of that instant; my father lifting his eyes from a letter, Elizabeth raising her fair head from her needle, the damp light falling upon the black characters of my treasure as I laid it before him and entreated his admiration. "See, father," I cried, in my eagerness, "how this man hath found what our teachers only dream of; teach me to follow him, for surely here is the secret which I have desired to divine since first I contemplated tempest and calm among our Alps."

Alphonse Frankenstein expounds Agrippa's exploded errors to Victor Frankenstein beside the inn window, and he did so not with that cursory glance which leaves a child unconvinced, but with a patience and a gravity which I had seldom seen him bestow upon my studies. He drew me to sit beside him, though the rain beat loudly, and bade me open where I would; then, passage by passage, he shewed me the nature of my delusion. He told me, in language tempered to my years yet wanting nothing in reason, that Agrippa had lived before true inquiry had purged itself of fable; that his principles had been tried by later men and found chimerical, because they attributed to words and to unproved virtues what belongs only to patient experiment; that a modern system had arisen, possessing powers real and practical precisely because it renounced such promises, and contented itself to dissect, to weigh, to measure, to doubt, until Nature herself should answer. "My dear Victor," said he, taking my hand in his, while Elizabeth listened with that serious and satisfied spirit which ever adorned her, "do not waste the ardour which I love in thee upon this sad though ingenious trash; not because I forbid thy curiosity, which is the gift of heaven, but because these authors will mislead it. If thou wouldst command lightning, thou must first learn what lightning is; if thou wouldst banish disease, thou must study the frame which disease afflicts. Glory obtained by incantation is a vapour; knowledge obtained by labour is an inheritance."

I felt the blood mount to my cheeks; for I perceived, with a sudden clearness, that he was indeed acquainted with the contents he condemned, and that his censure proceeded not from indifference but from understanding. Elizabeth looked upon me with a smile, gentle, unreproaching, yet full of that sympathy which was ever ours; and I, who had expected either indulgence or a cold dismissal, found myself disarmed by reason clothed in affection. Victor Frankenstein lays the Agrippa volume aside upon the inn shelf near Elizabeth Lavenza, restoring it to its place among the forgotten books while she watched, and the act, slight as it was, seemed to me weighty as a vow. I did not cast it from me in anger, nor did I caress it in secret; I set it upright, closed its clasps, and turned from it as one turns from a path which a trusted guide has pronounced impassable. "You are right, father," I said, though my voice faltered with the pain of relinquished marvels; "I will trouble myself no more with ghosts which never answer, but will return with greater ardour to those former studies which promise truth, however slowly."

Oh! exquisite pleasure still attends the memory of that tranquillity which followed my relinquishing of those ancient and latterly tormenting studies. My father pressed my shoulder, well pleased; Elizabeth, whose aerial creations of the poets had never required the philosopher's stone to render them lovely, rejoiced that my vehemence was subdued to a semblance of her own gentleness. For my own part, I experienced none of that sullen hunger which drives a boy back in secret to a forbidden author; I had been convinced, and conviction, when planted by love, takes deeper root than fear. What my father had taken the pains to explain, no curiosity could afterwards unsettle; and thus, by such slight ligaments as a rainy forenoon and half an hour of discourse, was I bound, as I then fondly believed, to prosperity.

***

When we returned to our house in Geneva, and afterwards to our *campagne* on Belrive, that eastern shore of the lake at rather more than a league from the city where our lives were passed in considerable seclusion, my first care was not, as it otherwise might have been, to procure Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus and to study their wild fancies with delight. I left those treasures, known I had imagined to few besides myself, untouched in the obscurity which justly belonged to them. In their stead I entreated my father to furnish me with those works which treat of secure foundations; Euclid, whose demonstrations admit of no appeal to authority; the commentaries upon Sir Isaac Newton, who had felt, like a child picking up shells beside a great and unexplored ocean of truth, yet had gathered shells of real pearl; and such introductions to mathematics and to the branches appertaining to that science as might discipline a mind too prone to soar.

My temper, though sometimes violent and my passions vehement, had ever been turned not towards childish pursuits but to an eager desire to learn; and now that desire, deprived of its unwholesome nourishment, fastened with a more intense application upon objects worthy of it. I was indifferent, as before, to the multitude of my school-fellows; but I united myself in the bonds of the closest friendship to one among them, and that one repaid my confidence with a generosity peculiarly his own. Henry Clerval was the son of a merchant of Geneva, a boy of singular talent and fancy, deeply read in books of chivalry and romance, who composed heroic songs and sought to make us act plays drawn from Roncesvalles and the Round Table. While my companion contemplated with a serious spirit the virtues of heroes and the actions of men, dreaming to become one among those gallant benefactors of our species whose names are recorded in story, I delighted, even as Elizabeth delighted in the majestic appearances of things, in investigating their causes; only now I pursued causes by number and by measure, not by incantation.

Victor Frankenstein traces mathematical diagrams with Henry Clerval in the bright Belrive garden, and I dwell upon that picture because it contains the whole temper of those two happy years. The lake lay blue and tranquil beneath us; the air was filled with the life and turbulence of our Alpine summer; bees laboured among the thyme, and the distant Jura lifted its calm line against the heavens. Upon a flat stone we had spread a paper, weighted at the corners with pebbles, and I, with compasses borrowed from a surveyor, described circles and triangles while Henry, who loved enterprise for its own sake, held the sheet against the breeze and laughed at my pedantry. "Thou wouldst reduce Mont Blanc to a problem, Frankenstein," cried he, with his animated gaze and easy bearing; "yet I love to see thee so humane in thy geometry, for thou explainest as if the figures themselves were friends." And Elizabeth, seated beneath the acacia with her work, lifted her cloudless blue eyes to bless and animate us, saying that she at last understood my rapture, since gladness akin to epic poetry might indeed arise when hidden laws were unfolded without deformity or terror.

No human being could have passed a happier childhood than myself during that interval; my parents were possessed by the very spirit of kindness and indulgence, and we felt that they were not tyrants to rule our lot according to caprice, but the agents and creators of all the many delights we enjoyed. My father, who was not himself scientific, yet watched my progress with a benevolent vigilance; he procured instruments, he questioned my masters at Geneva concerning the routine of education, he suffered me no longer to struggle, to a great degree self-taught, with a child's blindness added to a student's thirst. Elizabeth shone like a shrine-dedicated lamp in our peaceful home; her soft voice, her sweet glance, subdued what was rough through the ardour of my nature. And Clerval — could aught ill entrench upon the noble spirit of Clerval? He became, under her unfolding of the real loveliness of beneficence, more perfectly humane, more thoughtful in his generosity, even amidst his passion for adventurous exploit; and I, in return, learned from him to clothe my inquiries in language which men might love, for he reproved my tendency to a cold and solitary abstraction.

Yet ambition, though diverted from one channel, is not thereby extinguished; it seeks, like a mountain river, another course, and swelling as it proceeds, may become a torrent not the less destructive for flowing within lawful banks. For I confess that neither the structure of languages, nor the code of governments, nor the politics of various states possessed attractions for me; it was still the secrets of heaven and earth that I desired to learn, whether outward substance or inner spirit. Only now I desired them lawfully, patiently, and therefore, as I fatally reasoned, more surely. Wealth I despised as an inferior object; but what glory, I asked in my nightly meditations, would attend the discovery if I, not by elixir dreamed by unadepts floundering in multifarious knowledge, but by diligent anatomy and by the new philosophy of electricity and galvanism, could banish disease from the human frame and render man invulnerable to any but a violent death! The vision was the same which Agrippa had kindled; the fuel only was changed, from fable to fact, and therefore burned with a steadier and more consuming flame.

***

When I was about fifteen years old we had retired to our house near Belrive, when we witnessed a most violent and terrible thunderstorm, such as the Alps engender when heat long gathered bursts from behind the mountains of Jura. I remained, while the storm lasted, watching its progress with curiosity and delight, standing at the door while Elizabeth clung lightly to my sleeve and Henry shouted with admiration at each dazzling flash. On a sudden we beheld a stream of fire issue from an old and beautiful oak which stood about twenty yards from our house; and so soon as the dazzling light vanished, the oak had disappeared, and nothing remained but a blasted stump, reduced the next morning, as we found upon visiting it, not splintered by shock but entirely to thin ribbons of wood. I never beheld anything so utterly destroyed, and the scent of scorched fibre hung upon the damp air.

Victor Frankenstein watches lightning shatter the oak beside Elizabeth Lavenza outside Belrive house, and that gaze was no longer the gaze of a disciple mourning the overthrow of his lords of imagination; for Agrippa and Paracelsus were already dead within me, and their fall cast no shadow. Before this catastrophe I was not unacquainted with the more obvious laws of electricity; but on this occasion a man of great research in natural philosophy was with us, and excited by the event, he entered upon the explanation of a theory which he had formed upon electricity and galvanism, which was at once new and astonishing. He spoke of fluids, of conductors, of the animal frame as a machine susceptible to invisible powers; he shewed us, by a small apparatus he carried, how a lifeless limb might be made to contract, how the might which had ribbed the oak could be conducted, divided, stored. Elizabeth shuddered at the convulsive motion, yet listened; Henry marvelled that such terror could be rendered obedient; but I — I felt my heart expand with a hope more dangerous than any incantation had afforded. All that he said did not throw into shade my former idols, for they were already shade; it illuminated, as with that very lightning, a road which appeared secure, practicable, built upon foundations which no refutation could shake.

I plied the philosopher with questions until my father smiled at my importunity; I followed him after supper to the parlour, where the candles burned low, and entreated him to direct my reading. He complied with a kindness which Waldman himself could not afterwards have exceeded, advising a course of modern authors, warning me against haste, yet confirming that diligence might achieve what boastfulness only pretended. That night I could not sleep for gladness akin to rapture; tempest and calm, the silence of winter which would soon succeed our summer, the sublime shapes which surrounded our Swiss home, all seemed to address me with a new voice, promising that Nature, whose immortal lineaments no dissector had yet unveiled beyond secondary grades, might yield to one who approached her not as a sorcerer but as a son.

In the Geneva study, some weeks thereafter, when autumn had thinned the vines at Belrive and we had resumed our residence in town, I sought my father alone. The room was lined with those books of history and of moral inquiry which he loved; the fire burned low; without, the lake reflected a cold and cloudless sky. Victor Frankenstein pledges sober natural philosophy before Alphonse Frankenstein in the Geneva study, standing erect with a volume of mathematics beneath his arm while his father regarded him with affectionate attention. "Father," said I, after we had spoken of Caroline, now some years dead, and of Elizabeth, whom you destine, as my mother once hoped, for my future union, "I thank you that you took the pains, at Thonon, to undeceive me concerning Agrippa; you preserved me from exploded systems and from a thousand contradictory theories in which I must otherwise have floundered. I now desire your blessing upon a different labour. I will pursue natural philosophy, not as an adept seeking ghosts or devils, but as a servant seeking causes; I will bestow years upon chemistry, upon anatomy, upon the powers which animate and which extinguish life. If I succeed, the benefit shall be mankind's; if I fail, I shall at least have failed upon the true road." My father rose, embraced me, and answered that such ambition, so tempered by duty and by affection for the living, deserved every encouragement which fortune and paternal authority could supply.

Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin. When I look back, it seems to me as if that almost miraculous change of inclination, wrought not by neglect but by reason, was the immediate suggestion of the guardian angel of my life; her victory was announced by an unusual tranquillity and gladness of soul which followed my obedience. Yet, O reader who hast known the ardour of youth conducted into lawful paths, consider what spirit now possessed me! I had learned to despise the chimerical, only to trust the real with an unqualified and idolatrous faith; I had exchanged masters who promised everything and could perform nothing, for a mistress who promises little and performs wonders, and I loved her with a jealous and exclusive devotion. Destiny was too potent, and her immutable laws had decreed my utter and terrible destruction; but the storm that was even then hanging in the stars would envelop me no longer as a bewildered child lost in a slough of fable, but as a disciplined and solitary man, armed with instruments, confident in method, and therefore far more capable of infusing a spark of being into lifeless matter — should that secret ever unveil itself to my unremitting search.

"A merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!"

The voice came through the fog of the counting-house before the man was fairly seen; then the door shut behind him, and Fred stood there with the frost on his coat and his face bright from walking. He had colour enough for three ordinary men, and breath enough, when he laughed, to stir the papers on the desk.

Scrooge looked up from his ledger. The figures before him were neat, hard, and satisfactory. They did not laugh. They did not glow. They stayed where a man's hand had put them, and asked nothing but to be added again.

"Bah!" said Scrooge. "Humbug!"

"Christmas a humbug, uncle? You don't mean that."

"I do. What right have you to be merry? You're poor enough."

"What right have you to be dismal? You're rich enough."

It was the old battle, fought with the old weapons, and Bob Cratchit, in the little cell beyond the open door, bent lower over his copying that he might not be seen to listen. His fire was one coal pretending to be a fire; his candle did more for his fingers than the grate; and his white comforter, which had come down below his waist for want of a great-coat, made him look as if he were wrapped up against the weather indoors and out.

Fred warmed his hands, though there was little enough to warm them at. "There are many things from which I might have derived good, by which I have not profited, I dare say. Christmas among the rest. But I have always thought of Christmas time as a good time; a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time; the only time I know of in the long calendar of the year when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely. And therefore, uncle, though it has never put a scrap of gold or silver in my pocket, I believe that it has done me good, and will do me good; and I say, God bless it!"

From the Tank there came, before Bob knew it was coming, a short involuntary clap of the hands.

He stopped. He poked at his coal, and put it out.

Scrooge raised his head. "Let me hear another sound from you," he said, "and you'll keep your Christmas by losing your situation."

Fred, who had no anger in him that a laugh would not carry off, turned again to his uncle. "Don't be angry. Come! Dine with us to-morrow."

In the book's ordinary course of things — no, in the ordinary course of that cold room — the answer should have flown out like a shot. Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, until the door was shut and the fog had Fred again. Scrooge's mouth opened upon the first of those words. His pen was in his hand. The ledger lay open at a sum which wanted only one line more to be complete.

He did not speak.

What stopped him, no man there could tell. It might have been the applause dying guiltily behind the door. It might have been Fred's face, which had his sister Fan's look in it when it was earnest, though Scrooge would have cut out his tongue sooner than say so. It might have been the sudden, offensive picture of his own rooms, his own gruel, his own chair drawn close to a handful of fire, waiting for him at the end of to-morrow as they waited at the end of every day.

"Dine," said Scrooge, slowly, "with you."

"To-morrow, uncle. Christmas Day. My wife will be delighted."

Scrooge put down the pen. The ink made a black star upon the blotting-paper.

"What time?" he said.

Bob Cratchit's quill ceased to scratch.

Fred stared, and then broke into such a laugh that the candle in the Tank seemed to jump in its socket. "Time? Three, uncle. Three o'clock. But come when you will — come at two, come at four, only come!"

"I said, what time," returned Scrooge, with great severity. "A man who makes an engagement should keep it. Three."

"Three!" cried Fred. "Ha, ha! Uncle, you have made me the happiest man in London!"

"I have done nothing of the kind. I have accepted an invitation to dinner. If the dinner is bad, I shall say so. If the company is foolish, I shall say so. If there is singing after it — "

"There is always singing after it."

"Then I shall very probably leave early."

Fred caught both his hands, and shook them as if they belonged to a pump. "Leave when you please, go when you please, grumble at every dish if it makes you comfortable, only let us see you at the table. My wife has heard me promise it so often that she lays your place in her head every year. This year she shall lay it in earnest."

Scrooge drew his hands away. "Kind regards to her. Good afternoon."

"Good afternoon? Uncle, it is the best afternoon in the year! A merry Christmas! A happy New Year! Bob, a merry Christmas to you, and to Mrs. Cratchit, and to every one of the children!"

He was gone, shaking Bob by the hand at the outer door, filling the cold court with his voice, and leaving behind him a clerk who looked as if somebody had opened a window in February and let in June.

Scrooge stared at the unfinished sum. "Bedlam," he muttered. "The man will retire me to Bedlam. Three o'clock. I shall be expected. Expected!" And he took up his pen again with the air of a man who has signed a bill he does not remember reading.

***

The two gentlemen who came next, with their lists and their hats in their hands, found Scrooge no softer for Fred's visit; indeed, a man who has surprised himself is apt to be doubly hard upon everybody else, for fear the world should think him changed.

"At this festive season of the year, Mr. Scrooge, it is more than usually desirable that we should make some slight provision for the Poor and destitute, who suffer greatly at the present time. Many thousands are in want of common necessaries; hundreds of thousands are in want of common comforts, sir."

"Are there no prisons?"

"Plenty of prisons."

"And the Union workhouses? Are they still in operation?"

"They are. Still, I wish I could say they were not."

"The Treadmill and the Poor Law are in full vigour, then? I'm very glad to hear it. I was afraid something had occurred to stop them in their useful course."

The gentleman with the pen looked at the gentleman without it. Fred's laughter seemed still to hang about the room, and perhaps they took courage from it.

"A few of us are endeavouring to raise a fund to buy the Poor some meat and drink, and means of warmth. We choose this time because it is a time, of all others, when Want is keenly felt, and Abundance rejoices. What shall I put you down for?"

"Nothing."

"You wish to be anonymous?"

"I wish to be left alone. I don't make merry myself at Christmas, and I can't afford to make idle people merry. I help to support the establishments I have mentioned; they cost enough; and those who are badly off must go there."

"Many can't go there; and many would rather die."

"If they would rather die, they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population. Good afternoon, gentlemen."

They went. Scrooge worked on with an improved opinion of himself for a full ten minutes, after which he found that he had added the same column three times and got three different answers. "Three o'clock," he said to the ledger. "Three o'clock," the ledger seemed to say back. He shut it with a snap.

When the hour for closing came, Bob stood in the doorway with his hat in his hands and the snuffed candle behind him.

"You'll want all day to-morrow, I suppose?"

"If quite convenient, sir."

"It's not convenient, and it's not fair. If I was to stop half-a-crown for it, you'd think yourself ill-used, I'll be bound. And yet you don't think me ill-used when I pay a day's wages for no work. A poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December! But I suppose you must have the whole day. Be here all the earlier next morning."

"Thank you, sir. I will, sir."

Bob paused. It was not his place to speak of his employer's engagements; he knew that as well as he knew his fifteen shillings a week and the price of every coal in the box. Yet Fred's hand was still warm in his, and there was Christmas Eve in the man's throat whether he would or no.

"I hope, sir — I hope you will have a very comfortable dinner to-morrow."

Scrooge looked at him over his spectacles. "Eh?"

"At your nephew's, sir. He mentioned — that is, I could not help hearing — "

"No, you could not help applauding. I remember. My nephew's house is none of your business, Cratchit."

"No, sir. Certainly not, sir."

"Then don't make it so."

"No, sir." Bob backed to the door, cheerful even in retreat. "A merry Christmas, sir, all the same."

"Good night," said Scrooge, which for him, on that evening, was a concession so large that he frowned at himself in the glass of the door as he went out.

Bob ran home to Camden Town to play at blindman's-buff, sliding once on Cornhill on the way, for the honour of the night. Scrooge took his melancholy dinner in his usual melancholy tavern, read the newspapers, conned his banker's book, and as he walked home through the fog to his chambers, counted the hours, against his will, to three o'clock to-morrow.

***

His rooms were dark, cold, and large for one man; rooms that had been Marley's, in a house that seemed to have lost its way up a yard and never found it out again. The knocker on the door was a large knocker, and nothing more. Scrooge looked at it, with his key in the lock, a second longer than he had ever looked at it before.

It changed. It was not a knocker. It was Marley's face, with the spectacles up on the ghostly forehead and a dismal light about it, as a bad lobster shines in a dark cellar.

Scrooge stared. The face stared, without anger, without moving. Then it was iron again.

"Pooh, pooh!" said Scrooge, and shut the door with a bang that echoed through every empty room above and every cask in the cellars below. He went through sitting-room, bedroom, and lumber-room. Nobody under the table, nobody under the bed, nobody in the dressing-gown hanging against the wall. He double-locked himself in — which was not his custom — put on his nightcap and slippers, and sat down to his gruel before a fire that would hardly have warmed a mouse with a cold in its head.

The Dutch tiles round the grate shewed him Cains and Abels, Pharaoh's daughters, Apostles putting off to sea in butter-boats. His thoughts would not stay on them. Three o'clock. A laid place. Fred's wife, whom he had never seen, laying a knife and fork for a man who had refused to look at her wedding with anything but a growl.

"Humbug," said Scrooge. "I can send a note in the morning. A cold. Business. Anybody would accept a cold."

A bell, a disused bell high in the room, began to swing.

It swung softly, then loudly; and every bell in the house rang with it, until the air was full of their clamour. They ceased together. Deep below, a chain dragged over casks; then it came up the stairs, nearer and nearer, and through the double-locked door, without a pause, came Marley: transparent, in his pigtail, waistcoat, tights, and boots, wound about with cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel.

The flame in the grate leaped up, as if it knew him, and fell again.

"How now!" said Scrooge, caustic and cold, though his hands had begun to shake. "What do you want with me?"

"Much! Ask me who I was."

"Who were you, then? You're particular, for a shade."

"In life I was your partner, Jacob Marley."

Scrooge tried his old defence — an undigested bit of beef, a blot of mustard, more gravy than grave — and found it would not serve. When the spectre unbound the kerchief from its head and let its jaw fall upon its breast, he dropped upon his knees and clasped his hands before his face.

"Mercy! Dreadful apparition, why do you trouble me?"

"It is required of every man," said the Ghost, "that the spirit within him should walk abroad among his fellowmen, and travel far and wide; and if that spirit goes not forth in life, it is condemned to do so after death. I wear the chain I forged in life. I made it link by link, and yard by yard. Is its pattern strange to you? Or would you know the weight and length of the strong coil you bear yourself? It was full as heavy and as long as this, seven Christmas Eves ago. You have laboured on it since."

"Jacob! Old Jacob Marley, tell me more. Speak comfort to me, Jacob!"

"I have none to give. I am here to-night to warn you that you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate; a chance and hope of my procuring, Ebenezer. You will be haunted by Three Spirits. Without their visits you cannot hope to shun the path I tread."

Scrooge's face fell. "Is that the chance and hope you mentioned? I think I'd rather not."

"Expect the first when the bell tolls One."

"Jacob," faltered Scrooge, and stopped, for a thought had come to him even there, kneeling on his own hearthrug before a dead man. "I have promised to dine to-morrow. With Fred. I promised this very day. Does that — is that nothing?"

The Ghost regarded him with its fixed, death-cold eyes. For the first time since it entered, the chain about its middle seemed, not lighter, but still.

"It is a door opened by your own hand, Ebenezer. What man walks through it, I may not tell. A promise is not a life. You kept your promises to the ledger, too. Hear me! My time is nearly gone. Look that, for your own sake, you remember what has passed between us."

Then the window rose, the night air filled with wandering phantoms who sought to help the living and had lost the power for ever, and Marley floated out among them, joining their lament. Scrooge closed the window and examined his double-locked door. The bolts were undisturbed.

He tried to say "Humbug!" and stopped at the first syllable. He went to bed without undressing, in a room where to-morrow had already sat down, laid its knife and fork, and begun to wait for him.

***

The Spirits came as Marley had foretold; and what they shewed him — the boy alone in the cold schoolroom, Fezziwig's ball, Belle's quiet "I release you," the Cratchits' goose and the child upon the stool, Fred's bright parlour, and at last a name upon a neglected stone — no telling here shall make smaller by haste. It is enough that when Scrooge woke, he was laughing and crying in the same breath, holding fast to his own bedpost as a drowning man holds to a spar.

"It's here! The bedpost is here! The curtains are here! I am here! Oh, Jacob Marley! Heaven and the Christmas Time be praised for this!"

He flung open the window. The morning was clear, cold, golden, and jubilant; the church bells were ringing as if they had all gone joyfully mad together.

"What's to-day?" he cried to a boy in Sunday clothes below.

"To-day? Why, Christmas Day."

"Christmas Day! I haven't missed it! The Spirits have done it all in one night — they can do anything they like. Of course they can. Hallo, my fine fellow! Do you know the poulterer's in the next street? Do you know whether they've sold the prize turkey that was hanging up there? Go and buy it, and tell 'em to bring it here by cab, and here's a shilling, and if you come back in less than five minutes here's half-a-crown!"

The boy was off like a shot. Scrooge, dressing in a tumult, laughing, stumbling over his own slippers, remembered, between a cravat and a waistcoat, the thing he had remembered all night.

"Three o'clock," he said aloud. "I promised at three, before I knew. Before I knew anything! Bless me, yes. It won't do to be late. It won't do to be expected, and late."

He wrote no note of excuse. He went out into streets where every man, woman, and child he passed seemed to be carrying Christmas about with them in their arms; and when he met one of the gentlemen of yesterday, portly and pleasant, with his list still in his hand, Scrooge took him by both hands before a word could be said.

"My dear sir, how do you do? I hope you succeeded yesterday. It was very kind of you. A merry Christmas to you, sir! Allow me to offer my apologies for yesterday, and — will you have the goodness — " Here he whispered in the gentleman's ear, a sum so large that the gentleman stepped back to look at him, as a man looks at a house he has known for years which has suddenly put out a bow window.

"Lord bless me! My dear Mr. Scrooge, are you serious?"

"If you please. Not a farthing less. A great many back-payments are included in it, I assure you."

The turkey went to Camden Town in a cab, for no man could carry it. Scrooge went to church, and patted children on the head, and questioned beggars, and looked down into kitchens and up into windows, and found that everything could yield him pleasure. At two o'clock he was walking towards Fred's street. At half-past two he was walking away from it, having no more notion of retreat than a snowball has of summer; but he could not be early. To be expected at three, and to arrive at half-past two, was a new kind of embarrassment, and Scrooge bore it by making a complete circuit of the square, greeting every watchman, crossing-sweeper, and errand-boy upon the way.

At ten minutes to three he stood before Fred's door, and looked at the knocker.

It was a knocker. It stayed a knocker. He laughed at it, gently, as at an old acquaintance who had once frightened him very much and was now only brass.

***

"Uncle!" 

The door was open before the echo of the knock had left it. Fred must have been watching for him from the window, or listening for him from the hall; he had his hand out, his face aflame, and behind him a bright room full of the smell of dinner and the sound of people turning in their chairs.

"Uncle, you have come! I told her you would come! My dear, here he is — here is my uncle Scrooge, come to dinner, as he promised, at three!"

Scrooge stood upon the mat with the cold still on his coat, and saw it all at once: the fire, the holly, the table, the glasses catching the light, and at the nearer end, laid as Fred had said it was laid in her head every year, a place for him. Knife, fork, plate, and chair, waiting without reproach.

Fred's wife came forward — a plump, laughing girl, with dimples and kind eyes — and took the hand her husband had not seized, as naturally as if she had taken it every Christmas of her life.

"I am so glad," she said. "Fred never would let me take the things away. He said the empty place spoilt his appetite worse than any company could."

"My dear," said Scrooge, and found, to his own astonishment, that the word came easily. "I have been a — I have kept that place empty a great many years. Longer than you have been laying it, I dare say. I am sorry for every one of them."

"Then sit in it now, uncle, and make them up to us."

They brought him in as if he were something precious that had been lost in the snow; they took his coat, they warmed his chair, they pressed upon him first the best of everything, and then, fearing he was not comfortable, the second-best of everything besides. There were Fred's sister-in-law, and her sisters, and friends whose names Scrooge caught and lost and caught again, and every one of them had been told that he would not come, and every one of them behaved as if his coming were the most ordinary happiness in the world.

He ate of the goose, and praised it, and ate of the pudding when it came in blazing, and praised that more, having no standard of comparison but hunger of another kind. He marvelled, quietly, at the room. It held less plate than his own sideboard, and more welcome than his whole house had held in twenty years. When Fred's wife played the harp, and sang a song which Fan used to sing — not well, for she laughed and was stopped by the others, and began again — Scrooge sat with his knife idle in his hand and let the years do what they would with him.

"You are thinking of somebody, uncle," said Fred, softly, at his elbow.

"I am thinking of your mother," said Scrooge. "She used to fetch me home. I never thanked her half enough. I never — " He cleared his throat, and examined the holly on the wall with great attention. "You have her look, Fred, when you are in earnest. It put me out of countenance to-day, in the counting-house. I believe it is why I said yes before I had sense enough to say no."

Fred said nothing. He put his hand, for a moment, upon his uncle's shoulder, and took it away again before it could be shaken off. It was not shaken off.

"She would have been pleased to see you at this table," he said.

"I hope she is pleased," said Scrooge. "I hope a great many people are pleased, who had small reason. Cratchit, now — Bob Cratchit will have had his dinner by this time. There was a turkey." A gleam of boyish mischief came into the old man's face. "A turkey as large as — as large as a boy. He will never know who sent it. Fred, I have learned a number of things in one night, and the size of turkeys is the least of them, but it is nothing to be ashamed of."

"Nothing at all, uncle."

"And to-morrow morning — " Scrooge stopped, for Bob was not Fred's business, any more than Fred's house had been Bob's that afternoon in the Tank; and then he went on, because it was Christmas, and the room was warm. "To-morrow morning I have business with Bob which has waited fifteen shillings' worth of years. Let it wait one night more. He is playing blindman's-buff, I hope, and tumbling over Tiny Tim's stool."

"Amen to that," said Fred, "whoever Tiny Tim may be."

***

After dinner there were games, as Fred had promised in the counting-house, and Scrooge, who had fully intended to leave early, found himself at Blindman's-buff pointing out, with shrill and unseemly delight, where the blindman ought not to go; at How, When, and Where, answering so readily that Fred's wife suspected him of having prepared himself beforehand, which he denied with the indignation of a man accused of studying for an examination; and at Yes and No, where, being thought of by the whole company, he discovered himself in twenty questions by way of being an animal, a live animal, a disagreeable animal, a savage animal, and an animal that growled and grunted, and lived in London, and was not made a show of.

"Uncle Scrooge!" cried Fred, helpless. "It is uncle Scrooge himself!"

"It was to have been a bear," said Scrooge, wiping his eyes. "I am told I bear a resemblance. I shall practise amiability upon bears, Fred, when I meet them in society. They shall not know me."

The laughter went round the room like a fire catching in dry holly. And then — for Fred would have his way in his own house, as his uncle was learning — the glasses were filled again, and Fred rose, with his wife's hand under his arm and his face grave for once beneath its mirth.

"I give you," said Fred, "a man who has kept us waiting at this table longer than any guest in London, and who is worth the waiting. I give you my uncle Scrooge, who promised to come, and came. A merry Christmas and a happy New Year to him, and long life to keep his promise at this table every year!"

Scrooge was upon his feet before he knew he had risen. The room, the fire, the young faces turned towards him, swam a little, as rooms will when a man has been out all day in a hard frost of his own making and comes suddenly near the blaze.

"Fred," he said, "and my dear niece" — the dimples answered him — "and all of you, who never saw me before to-day except to hear me called an ogre in a coat; I thank you. I thank you for the place you kept. I am not worth the waiting, but I am worth — no. I will say what I came to say, if I can find it."

He found it, not in the ledger, where nothing of the sort is ever entered.

"A merry Christmas to you all. I shall keep my promise. Next year, and the year after, if I am let; and if ever any of you has an empty place at a table, fill it, in Heaven's name, before it learns to stay empty. Now fill your glasses again, for I am going to be taught the words of that song, if your wife will have patience with a pupil who is older than the tune."

He sat down amid such applause as that small room could hold, with Fred's hand wringing his under the table, and the place that had been empty so many years full at last, and his own glass catching the firelight as he lifted it again, to learn.
