The young woman had made an end of her speech, and stood with her hands clasped hard before her black gown, and her eyes full of a brightness that reproached the fellow opposite more than any loud upbraiding could have done! Oh, what a small room it was to hold so great a reckoning! A clerk's parlour let for the evening, with a carpet bag upon the chair and a bonnet upon the table, and a fire gone down to a red core in the grate, that snapped and sank as if it too were listening! The Spirit's crown-light fell upon the mourning stuff and shewed every worn fold of it, and upon the young man's forehead, where the lines of care had begun to cut themselves before their season, and upon old Scrooge himself, who clutched at the Spirit's robe and muttered that he knew this hour, ay, that he had buried it and hoped it would not rise again!

"You have chosen," said Belle, in that low even tone which belongs to minds resolved when the heart is most against them, "another mistress in my stead, and one that will not share her throne. I was promised to a boy who was content to be poor and to win his way by steady labour; I am released by a man who counts his worth in coin and reckons poverty a shame. Take back your word, Ebenezer, and go free to the fortune you desire."

The younger Scrooge opened his mouth with the ready answer of a man practised in accounts, about prudence and the world's reproach and the folly of beginning married life without a competence; and the elder Scrooge, at the Spirit's side, nodded grimly, for he remembered the argument and had polished it through seven hungry years. But in the midst of the reckoning the young man's voice broke upon a word, and he looked at the girl's thin gloves, darned at the fingers, and at the little trunk packed for her lodging, and at the tears she would not suffer to fall; and down, in a heap that jarred the crazy floor, Young Scrooge kneels before Belle in the cold little back parlour beside the dying fire.

Think of it, reader! Not the erect moralist vindicating himself, but a lover upon his knees, with his coat-tails in the dust and his hands catching at her skirt, forgetful of dignity, of ledgers, of the world's laugh! The coals cast a sudden red upon his lifted face, and the damp upon the walls glistened, and the landlady's clock upon the mantel ticked louder, as if astonished at the condescension! "Do not leave me!" cried the young man, in broken sentences that tumbled over one another, for he spoke now as no counting-house pupil speaks, but as a boy speaks who fears the dark. "Say I have been cold, say I have been grasping, and I will unlearn it upon my knees! Marry me poor, Belle, and teach me to be rich in the way you mean! If you go, I shall harden into what you fear, and call it wisdom; if you stay, I may yet be saved from myself! Oh, do not give me up to gain! Stay, stay, and chide me when I wander!"

Old Scrooge gave a great start, for this was no part of the memory he had nursed; and he turned upon the Spirit with a look of wild appeal, as if to ask whether shadows might be taught new speeches. The Ghost's face, wherein many former faces seemed blended and dissolved, regarded him fixedly and said nothing; only the jet of light above its brow burned steadier, as a lamp burns when the oil is stirred.

Belle trembled exceedingly, and drew back a pace, and then stood fast; for a woman who truly loves cannot hear such prayer unmoved, though prudence plucks at her sleeve. She looked upon the kneeling figure, upon the eager restless eyes that gain had not yet wholly dimmed, upon the hands that shook not with age but with youth's terror of loss; and pity, and old affection, and that dangerous hope which tells a good heart that it may reform what it cherishes, warred within her breast. She stooped, she caught his wrists in her small firm grasp, she bade him rise and not shame himself before Heaven; and Belle raises young Scrooge upright in the cold little back parlour beside the fire.

"Ebenezer," she said, softly, yet with a steadiness that made the elder listener bow his head, "I will not abandon you in your struggle, if struggle it be. Keep your promise, and I will keep my troth. But mark me! If ever I find that I must beg for a little of your time as a pauper begs for bread, then this hour shall witness against us both. Love me better than money, and I am yours through want and plenty."

He swore it, with kisses upon her hands that left the dust of the floor upon them, and with vows poured out in the extravagance of reprieve; and she smiled through her tears and suffered the trunk to be unstrapped and the bonnet to be set aside. The fire, as if enlivened by the compact, threw up a sudden tongue of flame that reddened the low ceiling; the clock struck with a more cheerful note; even the landlady's cat, stealing in for warmth, arched its back and purred against Belle's gown! Old Scrooge laughed and wept together, and clapped his thin hands, and cried to the Spirit that it was well done, ay, nobly mended, though he knew not whether he spoke to the Ghost or to his own youth.

***

The snow lay deep upon the steps when next the light commanded, and the sexton was sweeping it with a birch broom, grumbling at Christmas weddings that kept honest men from dinner! Within, the air smelt of damp prayer-books and orange-peel and the hot wax of two choir candles; the breath of the few witnesses rose in little clouds; the clerk stamped his feet to keep them warm. Belle came in upon her father's arm, no longer in mourning but in a grey gown turned and pressed for the occasion, with a knot of white ribbon at her throat that her mother had lent her, and a face pale with cold and resolve! Young Scrooge waited, sprucer than his means allowed, with a new cravat bought upon credit and his hair wetted down, shifting from foot to foot as boys will when the parson is late!

Belle and young Scrooge stand together before the altar in the small city church. Mark them well! The parson's voice droned through the responses, now drowned by a gust that shook the windows, now clear again; the ring, a plain gold circle that had been Belle's grandmother's, stuck for a moment upon the knuckle hardened by pen-holding, and then slipped home; the bride's fingers closed upon it as upon an anchor! They knelt upon the worn hassocks, they rose when bidden, they signed their names in the damp register with a pen that sputtered, he in a bold clerkly hand, she in a small neat character that seemed to promise order in a household! The witnesses — a fellow apprentice with ink upon his cuff, a cousin in a patched shawl — pressed forward with hearty good wishes and with *cold* noses; the sexton held the door for his fee; the snow received them with a cheerful crunch as man and wife!

Old Scrooge capered in the aisle, unseen and unheard, and blessed the parson, and blessed the sexton, and would have kissed the bride had the shadow suffered it! "Spirit!" he cried, catching the luminous robe in both his hands, "hear me! I was a fool to reckon happiness by interest! She will be my thrift, my conscience, my home! Fezziwig himself never made so good a bargain!" The Ghost of Christmas Past bent its child-like brow upon him, and its voice came as from a great distance, low and sorrowful. "Take heed," it said, "for the bargain must be kept."

***

Seven years were swallowed in the waving of the Spirit's hand, as a sum is swallowed in a total; and the snow of the wedding had given place to the soot of London and the rattle of carts upon Holborn! A counting-room, narrow and ill-lighted, with a desk stained by many elbows, and shelves of ledgers bound in vellum, and a single lamp with a cracked chimney that smoked and stank! Upon the desk lay open a day-book, ruled in red, where figures stood in dismal columns like soldiers awaiting orders! Behind the desk sat Scrooge, no longer young, with the first grey threading his temples and the first hardness settling about his mouth; before the desk stood his wife, with a shawl drawn about shoulders thinned by nursing, and a sleeping infant wrapped against her bosom, whose breath came short and loud in the close air!

Belle faces young Scrooge across the ledger in the cramped counting-room beside the smoky lamp. Oh, fatal furniture for a marriage! The lamp threw its yellow upon the vellum and left their faces half in gloom; the infant stirred and whimpered; the rain beat upon the unwashed skylight! "Come home to supper," she pleaded, with that patience which is more terrible than anger, "for the boy has coughed all day and asks for his father, and the fire is low, and Christmas is at hand. Marley may spare you an hour; surely mankind may spare so much?" He answered without lifting his pen, reckoning as he spoke, that coal was dear and custom slack and rent due at quarter-day, and that a man with a family upon his hands must labour while his strength lasts, lest they come upon the parish! She answered that a child needs a father's laugh more than a new gown, and that she had mended the old curtains to keep out the draught, and had pawned — here she faltered — had pawned her mother's ribbon for milk! He winced, and dipped his pen deeper, and said she did not understand business, and that affection would not pay the baker!

Then did the elder Scrooge, who had watched with growing horror, thrust himself between them, though they knew him not, and cry aloud to his former self to shut the book, to take the wife in his arms, to be Fezziwig for an hour rather than Marley for a lifetime! In vain! The shadow went on casting up its figures, and the wife stood with the babe against her heart, and the lamp smoked on, indifferent as fate! Marley himself put his head in at the door, with his great jaw bound in flannel for the toothache, and grinned at the domestic tableau, and asked if lovers' quarrels paid interest! The young husband laughed uneasily and bent lower over his task, to shew diligence before his partner; the wife turned away, lest the tears fall upon the child!

"Spirit!" groaned the old man, wringing his hands, "I see it! I, who feared want for myself, have taught him to fear it double for wife and child, until fear has become worship! She stayed to save me, and I am dragging her into the pit with my industry! Remove this sight! I cannot bear the good I have spoiled!"

The Ghost pointed with its small strong hand to the ledger, where the figures swam and multiplied; to the wife's darned cuff; to the infant's laboured breath! "These are the shadows of the things that have been," it said, in its far-off murmur, "and of the seed sown in that parlour hour. Would you unsee what staying has cost?"

***

He was in his own bedroom again, or so it seemed, for the curtains loomed about him and the Dutch tiles of the fireplace glimmered faintly, and the cold struck through his dressing-gown to the bone! The Spirit stood before him, grown dimmer, as a candle stands when the air is exhausted, yet its light still poured from its crown in a clear unbroken jet that dazzled his aching eyes! He hated the light, for it shewed him Belle's ribbon in pawn and the child's cough and his own younger face grown sharp with calculation! He seized, in sudden fury and terror, the great extinguisher-cap that hung beneath the Spirit's arm, and with both his withered hands Scrooge grasps the extinguisher above the Ghost of Christmas Past in the dark bedroom.

Down he forced it, with curses and prayers jumbled together, crushing the bright hair, smothering the summer flowers that trimmed the white tunic, striving to blot out memory as a debtor blots a sum! The cap covered the whole slight form; the struggle shook the bed-curtains till the rings rattled upon the rods! Yet, press as he might till his knuckles whitened and his breath came in sobs, the light streamed from beneath in a hundred fiery threads, darted through the keyhole, gilded the gruel-cup upon the hob, and painted Belle's face upon the darkness before him, younger and older at once, reproachful and tender! He was conscious of a deadly faintness, of the floor sinking beneath his slippers, of a rushing in his ears as of wind through a churchyard yew!

***

The wind was indeed blowing, keen and salt, through rank grass and among leaning stones! An iron gate, rusted upon its hinges, clanged behind him; the snow lay in patches, half thawed, shewing the black earth beneath like mourning through a worn coat! The Spirit, now scarcely more than a luminous mist, stood beside a low mound where no stone yet stood, only a little wooden cross with a name half washed away by rain! Beside it knelt a woman in a widow's shawl — for Belle's father was dead — worn and thin, but beautiful still in sorrow, laying a sprig of holly upon the frozen earth! No husband stood beside her; no child's voice called her mother; the city lay far off, indifferent, its smoke staining the winter sky!

Scrooge reaches toward Belle through darkness in the empty snow-covered churchyard beyond the iron gate. He forgot that he was but a gazer at shadows; he forgot the Spirit, the night, his own age; he stumbled forward with arms extended, his nightcap fallen from his head, his feet slipping upon the stones, crying in a voice cracked with weeping that she should not kneel alone, that he was coming, that he would shut the ledger for ever if she would but look upon him! The wind took his words and scattered them among the graves! Belle rose, drew her shawl closer about her throat, gazed for a moment with empty eyes toward the place where he stood — and saw nothing, for the living cannot see the dead-alive who haunt their past! She turned, she passed through the gate, her footsteps dying upon the hard road that led back to the cold rooms and the coughing child and the husband poring over figures by a smoking lamp!

The Spirit raised its drooping hand, and the light that had tormented him flickered low, as if spent by what it had revealed! "One whom you loved has stayed," it murmured, "and learn what staying bears when gain remains the master. Shall the past plead further, or will you carry its reckoning forward?" Old Scrooge fell upon his knees among the weeds, clutching at the holly she had left, and swore, not as young men swear upon altars, but as old men swear upon graves, that he would wrestle with his idol yet! The snow began anew to fall, softening the mound, hiding his footprints, leaving the churchyard to its silence!

Anne enters the Great House drawing-room and meets Captain Wentworth formally before the assembled Musgrove family.
Seated opposite Wentworth at dinner, Anne hears his naval history and answers his guarded enquiries about Kellynch.
After dinner Anne plays the piano-forte while Wentworth watches Louisa and Henrietta press him for dances.
Alone briefly by the tea-table, Anne and Wentworth speak of altered places and find neither can be easy.
Returning through the dark lane, Anne learns Wentworth will breakfast near the Cottage and resolves not to flee him.

The apothecary had been gone an hour, and little Charles slept at last, his small face turned upon the pillow and one hand still restless against the coverlid whenever a stair creaked or a door was allowed to fall too heavily in the passage. Mary stood beside the bed with her shawl drawn close, though the room was warm, and looked from the child to Anne with the injured air of one who had already borne more than could fairly be required of her.

"He will wake and want me, and then he will kick, and then Mr Robinson's work will all be undone, and Charles will say I ought to have kept him quiet. I am sure I do not know how any mother can be expected to have nerves for such a thing. You saw me yesterday, Anne. I was quite overset."

Anne folded the damp cloth which she had laid aside and placed it upon the wash-stand where Jemima might find it. "He has taken the draught. Jemima understands that he is not to be lifted, and that the room is to be kept still. If he wakes in pain, you must send to the Great House directly."

"Send!" cried Mary. "And who is to go? And what am I to do till somebody comes? Oh, Anne, do not talk as if it were all settled, when I feel I shall be quite ill with listening for him. Charles says his father expects him, and expects me too, I dare say, though nobody ever thinks of what I suffer; and here is Captain Wentworth to be met, and everybody will be acquainted with him but me."

"You cannot leave your child to-night, Mary."

"I did not say I could. I say it is very hard that I cannot. And it is harder still that you should be going to sit here in comfort—"

She stopped, not from any sense of injustice in the word, but because little Charles stirred and sighed in his sleep. Jemima, seated in the corner with her work dropped in her lap, rose without speaking and shaded the candle with her hand. The child settled again.

Anne looked at her sister, at the tired, careful maid, at the quiet room. The duty which had seemed so plain in the first alarm had altered with the apothecary's assurances. She was not wanted here as she had been yesterday; she was wanted, if the truth must be owned even to herself, nowhere at all, except as an excuse by which Mary might complain with greater liberty. At the Great House, half a mile off, Frederick Wentworth was by this time perhaps already arrived. To remain would be safety of a kind. To go would be to place herself where no occupation could protect her from being seen, and from seeing that she was no longer anything to him.

She heard herself speak before the resolution had taken any comfortable shape. "Then I shall go with Charles."

Mary stared. "You?"

"Mrs Musgrove will think it strange if none of us appear. Charles may tell them how little Charles is going on. You will stay here, where Jemima can be with you every moment, and you may send the man over if there is any change. I shall be within call."

"Dear me, Anne, I did not mean—" Mary's countenance brightened even while she protested. "Though to be sure, if I am left here quite alone with a sick child, when I have not nerves—"

"You will not be alone. And you will be in your own room, and may lie down when he sleeps."

"Well," said Mary, sinking upon the sofa with a sigh that expressed both martyrdom and relief from the necessity of dressing, "if you insist upon going, I suppose I must submit to be left. Only you will tell Mamma Musgrove that I would have come if I had been less anxious, and that nobody knows what a mother feels. And Anne—if Captain Wentworth should enquire after me, you may say I am very much confined by my poor boy."

Anne went upstairs to change her gown with hands that would perform their office and a mind that reproached her for every trembling movement. She had chosen it. That was the circumstance which no reasoning could soften. She had not been detained by a duty; she had walked, by her own act, toward the meeting she had believed herself so fortunate in escaping.

***

The Great House was all light and expectation when Charles handed her in from the carriage, though the distance had scarce required one. In the hall there were voices, the smell of dinner already upon the stairs, and Louisa's laugh from the drawing-room, clear and unembarrassed; and then Charles opened the door, and Anne saw him.

Captain Wentworth stood near the fire with Mr Musgrove, one hand resting upon the back of a chair, in the very act of answering some hearty question concerning a road or a horse. He turned as they entered. Eight years had not diminished him. They had given breadth to his shoulders and confidence to his air, and had burnt into his face a colour which the drawing-room candles only made more glowing; but the eyes, the mouth, the sudden attention of the whole countenance—those were what she remembered, and for an instant the room had no other person in it.

Mr Musgrove came forward with both hands extended. "Miss Anne! This is kind indeed. We feared we should have none of the Cottage party but Charles. How is the poor little fellow, eh? And Mary—Mary bears it, I hope? Ah, Captain Wentworth, this is Miss Anne Elliot. You have met Sir Walter's family, I think, in former days—somewhere in the county, was it not?"

"I had that pleasure," said Captain Wentworth.

He bowed. She curtseyed. The words were perfectly civil, and the bow neither more nor less than the occasion required, and Anne felt, with a composure that surprised her, that she could answer Mrs Musgrove's pressing enquiries about the child, could say that the collar-bone had been replaced, that Mr Robinson apprehended no present danger, and that Mary remained at home. Henrietta hung upon her arm with real concern. Louisa demanded whether little Charles had cried very much, and whether he had asked for her.

All this gave her time. When she looked again, Captain Wentworth was speaking to Charles about dogs, as easily as if no third person in the room had ever cost him a thought. His indifference, if it was indifference, was at least a protection. She might sit through an evening under its shelter, unseen while she saw everything.

It was not quite so, however. Once, while Mrs Musgrove was lamenting that so promising an evening should have been clouded by an accident, his glance crossed Anne's, and fled—not in confusion, she thought, but in the settled purpose of a man who has determined what he will not feel. She accepted the sentence. It was what she had expected. It was only wonderful that expectation could prepare her so little.

***

At dinner Anne found herself placed between Mr Musgrove and Charles, with Captain Wentworth nearly opposite, a circumstance owing to Louisa's active arrangement of the party in the doorway; Louisa herself was on his right, Henrietta on his left, and both sisters were in that state of delighted attention which left their mother to observe, with much complacency, that young people always understood one another.

Mr Musgrove pressed his guest to approve the strong ale, to pronounce upon the mutton, to hear the history of a tenant who had been ruined by keeping too many harriers, and to say when the shooting at Uppercross might be expected to repay a man for the dulness of being ashore. Captain Wentworth answered everything with spirit. He praised the ale, he laughed at the tenant, he spoke of shooting as a landsman's amusement which a sailor learned to value by being so often without it.

"You must not judge us too hardly, sir," said he, "for talking of our profession as if the world were made of salt water. A man who has lived in a frigate learns to think a dry coat and a dinner that does not slide off the table very great luxuries."

"And very right too," cried Mr Musgrove. "We owe you fellows more than we can say. There is my poor Dick—"

His wife's hand was upon his arm in a moment. He recollected himself, coughed, and called for more gravy; but the pause had been enough to shew Anne the change in Captain Wentworth's face. The gaiety was gone out of it. He leaned a little forward.

"I knew your son, sir, for a short time, under Captain Harville. He was a fine lad."

It was simply said, and Mr Musgrove nodded with his eyes suddenly wet, and Mrs Musgrove, after a silence in which the servants moved very softly, began to speak of Dick as she always spoke of him now, with that large, unguarded grief which company both pitied and avoided. Captain Wentworth listened. He asked whether a miniature, which she mentioned, had been taken before the boy went first to sea; he remembered the name of a midshipman who had been Dick's friend; and Anne, watching the proud, bright face made gentle by another's sorrow, found the pain of the evening alter its character. This was the man she had known. His resentment might be hers to bear, but his heart had not been narrowed by success.

Louisa could not endure a long gravity. "Captain Wentworth must tell us about the Asp. Charles says it was the most dreadful storm, and that you would not leave the deck."

"Charles gives me credit for what every man on board performed as a matter of course."

"Oh, but the particulars! Were you really afraid the ship would go down?"

"I was too busy, Miss Louisa, to have leisure for conclusions. A sloop in a gale off St Domingo affords a man occupation enough for his fears."

He told it, nevertheless—not boastfully, but with that vivid economy of speech which made the wind audible in the quiet dining-room, the seas breaking over a little vessel, the men at the pumps, the dawn coming at last upon wreck and exhaustion. Henrietta forgot her plate. Charles interposed questions of tonnage and guns which no lady could be expected to comprehend. Anne heard every word while appearing to attend to Mr Musgrove's account of a drain in the lower meadow; and when, in the course of the tale, Captain Wentworth said that he had written home from Bermuda with a certainty of being understood by those who awaited him, his eye did not seek hers. That certainty belonged to a world in which she had no place.

Afterwards, as if some recollection made abruptness necessary, he turned to her for the first time with a direct enquiry. "Kellynch is let, I understand, Miss Elliot. My sister is very comfortably established there."

"She appears to be so, sir. Admiral Croft and Mrs Croft have made themselves much liked in the neighbourhood."

"Sophia is easily pleased where she has room to be useful. She speaks of the house as wanting nothing but a little less ceremony in the breakfast parlour."

"Then she will have improved it," said Anne, and was rewarded by the nearest approach to his old smile.

It vanished as he replied, "Places alter less than the people who return to them."

No one else appeared to hear any particular meaning. Louisa claimed him for the end of a story about a curate's horse, and the moment was gone.

***

When the ladies withdrew, Anne had the relief of Mrs Musgrove's accounts of neighbours, medicines, and Christmas dinners past and to come; but relief of that sort had its limits, and when the gentlemen joined them the room was again arranged by forces not her own. The piano-forte stood open. Louisa, who played with great spirit and very little attention to the feelings of a song, was called upon first, and performed a march with such energy that her mother declared it made her quite warm. Henrietta sang. Then there was a cry for country dances, though the party was too small to make a set with any propriety, and Charles proposed that they should push back the carpet.

"Miss Elliot plays these things so well," said Henrietta, turning. "Anne, do sit down. You know all the tunes Mary likes."

It was an old office, familiar and unthanked, and Anne took her place without objection. The music gave her hands employment and her face a direction away from the dancers. Louisa flew through the figures with Captain Wentworth, laughing when he mistook a turn, instructing him with an authority which delighted him; Henrietta and Charles completed what set they could; Mr Musgrove beat time against his knee and assured the company that this was better than any ball in Bath.

Between tunes Captain Wentworth came to the instrument to turn a page which did not require turning. "You play as you used to do, Miss Elliot."

The words were low, and spoken without looking at her. Anne's fingers found the next air of themselves. "I have had more practice in playing for others than in dancing."

"That is an arrangement society often makes for those who can be useful."

"Usefulness has its consolations, sir."

"For the useful, perhaps. I have seldom seen it consulted." He moved away to be claimed by Louisa, who declared that the next dance was promised to nobody and therefore must be his.

Anne played on. She played correctly, steadily, with a precision which nobody remarked because it was expected; and under the cover of her employment she could observe what she would not for the world have appeared to watch: his ease with both sisters, the frank admiration in Louisa's eye, Henrietta's softer pleasure, and his own evident disposition to be pleased. He had come into the county, as she had heard, a man ready to settle, meaning to choose quickly and not repining for what was lost. Any pleasing young woman, perhaps—her mind supplied what pride would once have supplied for her. If Louisa's liveliness could fix him, Anne should see it happen night after night, in rooms where her part would still be at the piano-forte, furnishing the music for other people's happiness.

The thought came with so distinct an image that her hand faltered on a repeated note. Louisa, breathless, laughed at the mistake; Captain Wentworth looked round. Anne began again instantly, and played the tune through to its end without another error.

***

Tea interrupted the dancing, and with it came that scattering of a party which is often more dangerous than its closest order. Mrs Musgrove slept openly in her chair for five minutes and woke denying it. Mr Musgrove proposed cards. Louisa and Henrietta were examining a new pattern for trimming a bonnet at the far table, and Charles, discovering that the kettle had been allowed to cool, was in loud negotiation with a servant. Anne, pouring out tea, found Captain Wentworth beside her with an empty cup.

"For Mr Musgrove, if you please. He takes it strong."

She filled it. "You remember the customs of houses very readily, sir."

"Naval life teaches a man to learn a new ship quickly—or to be in everybody's way."

"You do not seem in anybody's way at Uppercross."

"That is the Musgroves' kindness. They make a stranger feel that he has been expected." He set down the cup, but did not immediately carry it away. "I was sorry to hear of your nephew's fall. Mrs Charles Musgrove must be very anxious."

"Mary is anxious; but we hope there will be no lasting injury. She wished to come herself, and could not persuade herself to leave him."

A slight movement at the corner of his mouth might have been disbelief, or only recollection of Mary's character through Charles's conversation. "You left her with assistance, I hope?"

"With Jemima, who is very steady. I can be fetched in a few minutes."

"You are always fetchable, Miss Elliot," he said, more abruptly than the occasion warranted. "Other people's convenience appears to arrange itself upon the supposition."

Anne felt the colour rise, and was glad of the teapot between them. "I hope I am not in the habit of complaining of arrangements which I have myself made."

"No. Complaining was never—" He stopped. Across the room Louisa called to him to come and decide whether blue or green ribbon became Henrietta best, with the confidence of a young woman who has no doubt of being obeyed. He answered her with ready gaiety, took up Mr Musgrove's tea, and left Anne standing by the urn.

She did not know whether he had intended reproach or kindness, and the uncertainty was worse than either. What was certain was that civility between them could not long preserve its disguise. Every sentence carried an old meaning under its new one, and every listener might be ignorant while they themselves understood too much.

***

The evening broke up early on account of the invalid at the Cottage. Charles would have had the carriage, though the October night was fine and the lane dry; Anne preferred to walk, and preferred it the more because Captain Wentworth, as they stood in the hall, announced his intention of being at the Great House to breakfast and go out with Charles in the morning.

"We shall call at the Cottage first, Anne," said Charles, pulling on his greatcoat. "My sisters are determined to see how the little fellow does, and Wentworth says he must enquire after Mary himself, since she was kept prisoner last night. Only a few minutes, you know. You need not be at the trouble of dressing the child up."

"Mary will be very much obliged by the attention," said Anne. It was all she could say. Captain Wentworth stood by the door with his hat in his hand, wishing Mr and Mrs Musgrove good night with a warmth she had once believed exclusively her own; Louisa was entreating him to be early, Henrietta repeating that the morning would be beautiful; and Anne, wrapping her shawl round her, had the sensation of having come through a danger only to learn that it would present itself again at breakfast, in daylight, without even the protection of a crowd at dinner.

The lane was dark under the trees, and the air smelt of wet leaves and wood-smoke from the cottages. Charles walked fast, full of his new friend. "A capital fellow, Anne. No nonsense in him. My father is quite taken with him, and as for the girls, Lord bless you, they will hear of no one else. He shoots to-morrow, and next week he is to shew us a way of getting over the low ground by Winthrop that I never thought of. I told him he must make Uppercross his home while he stays."

"You were all very kind to him."

"Kind! It is himself. Such a man as that might marry either of the girls, if he took a fancy. I should not object, I am sure. Though Henrietta and Hayter—well, that will settle itself. What did you think of him, Anne?"

The question came when the gate of the Cottage was already in sight, and one window shewed Mary's candle still burning. Anne kept her eyes upon that small, steadfast light.

"I thought him very much what the world must have made him," she said. "Confident, and warm, and—much altered in his circumstances."

"Altered!" cried Charles. "My father says he is improved in looks, too. There is no catching him shy, is there? But I dare say eight years at sea will cure any man of that."

Mary met them in the passage, eager, pale, and fully prepared with an account of having never closed her eyes, though Jemima was discovered asleep in the kitchen with her head upon her arms, and little Charles slept upstairs as peacefully as he had done at their departure. She must hear everything; who had sat where, what had been eaten, whether Captain Wentworth had enquired after her more than once, and whether he was handsomer than his sister. Anne answered until the clock struck, answering truly and yet leaving out the whole evening.

When at last she stood alone in her room, with Charles's promise sounding still in her ears and the morning already appointed against her wishes, she did not say that the worst was over. She untied her bonnet, laid it by, and began, with a steadiness she could not account for, to consider what gown she should wear at breakfast.

remixes.title: A Firmness Corrected
events: Anne refuses her own offer to stay, and Mary remains fretfully beside little Charles at the Cottage.
Anne enters the Great House parlour and finds Captain Wentworth already seated near the fire.
Across the dinner table, Wentworth speaks of the Asp while Anne answers his studied politeness.
After dinner, Anne plays country dances as Louisa demands Wentworth choose the next tune.
In the hall, Wentworth returns Anne's dropped glove and asks whether the child is safe.
Anne walks home through darkness, carrying his courteous words and knowing nothing is settled.

The wind came hard off the sea and took the ladies' shawls sideways as they gained the Cobb. The stone was damp under foot, and the little party from Uppercross stood a moment to admire the breadth of water, the white fret upon the waves, and the dark line of the cliffs beyond. Captain Harville, who had walked up with them to shew the place to the best advantage, named the vessels in the bay. Captain Wentworth was in high spirits; the exercise, the company, the return to a shore he understood, had given his countenance its full animation. Louisa Musgrove kept close by his side, her colour heightened, her eyes bright with the pleasure of novelty and of being understood.

They descended to the lower walk, and Louisa, laughing, held out her hands to be jumped down the flight which joined the two levels. Wentworth, indulgent as an elder brother might have been, took them and set her lightly upon her feet. She cried out with delight, and before the laugh was well done, she was gone from them again, running with quick light steps up the steep stairs to have the pleasure a second time.

"Let me try it again," she called, looking over her shoulder. "Do go back, Wentworth, and I will jump. You did it so well. Only a moment."

He had followed her with his eyes, smiling at first. The smile altered. The steps were wet. The wind plucked at her gown. A fishing-boat below knocked against the wall, and the sound came up sharp between the gusts.

"No," he said. "Not again, Miss Louisa."

She pouted, but with perfect good humour. "Oh! You are cruel. It was nothing. Come, you must. Henrietta did not half enjoy it, for she was behind. Let me shew her."

"I will not catch you," he said, and his voice, though still gay, had something decided which had not been there before. He did not put out his hands. He stood below, with his feet planted a little apart against the wind, and shook his head. "The stones are slippery. You came down very well, but a second trial is folly. Give me your hand and come down by the steps, and we shall walk on."

Louisa stared. The whole party had gathered; Mrs. Charles Musgrove exclaiming at the cold, her husband laughing, Miss Anne Elliot a few paces off with Captain Harville and Captain Benwick. To be refused, before them all, and by the very person who had praised decision above all things, was a check which Louisa had not learned to receive with grace.

"But you said a determined mind was the finest thing in the world," she said, her cheeks growing warmer. "You said nothing was to be done without it. And now, when I am determined, you call it folly."

Wentworth coloured. Anne, watching from the side, felt the remark strike him more than any reproof from an older head could have done. She saw his mouth press together, and his eyes go for an instant to the wet edge of the pavement where Louisa's half-boot stood close to the fall.

"I did say it," he answered, after a pause. "And I say it still. But determination is not running headlong when a friend tells you the footing is unsafe. If you will be firm, be firm in doing right. Come down. There is my hand. You shall have the credit of minding reason, which is harder than minding inclination."

He held up his hand, not to receive her spring, but to guide her. Louisa hesitated. The wind lifted a loose curl across her face. Behind Wentworth, Henrietta looked anxious; Charles called out, "Come on, Lou, do not be a child;" Mary declared she should catch her death standing there. Louisa glanced from one face to another, and found no ally for the jump. Even Captain Benwick, who seldom offered an opinion in company, murmured that the Captain was in the right, the steps wanted care.

It was a small humiliation, but to nineteen it seemed considerable. With an air between laughing and crying, she put her foot to the first step, then the second, holding Wentworth's hand very tight. He steadied her, his other arm half raised as if to guard her should she slip, and in a dozen careful paces she was upon the lower Cobb. Her gown was damp at the hem. Her gloves were soiled from touching the wall. She drew her hand away quickly.

"There," she said. "I am down. I hope you are satisfied. Nobody will call me resolute now."

"I shall," said Harville kindly, to cover the awkwardness. "A sailor knows when to shorten sail. That is resolution too." But Louisa would not be comforted just then. She walked on a little ahead with Henrietta, her head bent against the wind, and spoke low and fast, as one who must justify herself to a sister.

Wentworth remained where she had left him for a moment longer than was necessary, looking at his empty hand. Anne fancied — and checked herself for fancying — that he was surprised at his own steadiness. When he turned, he met her eye. Something in his expression, a consciousness, a half-apology for the lecture they had both heard him give only the day before upon the hazel nut and the firmness of Louisa's character, passed between them without words. He coloured again and addressed some remark to Harville about the tide.

They walked back towards the town in a body made ragged by the wind. Mary took Anne's arm and complained of Louisa's perversity and of Captain Wentworth's contradictoriness in the same breath. "First he puts her up to everything, and then he will not indulge her in the least thing. I am sure Louisa has a right to be vexed. Though, to be sure, if she had fallen, we should never have forgiven ourselves. My nerves could not have borne it. Did you see how near the edge she stood? I declare I was quite sick."

Anne soothed her as well as she could, while keeping her eyes upon the two figures ahead. Louisa had recovered enough to laugh, but the laugh was forced. Wentworth exerted himself to restore her good humour, pointed out a brig working out, told a story of a midshipman at Plymouth who had leapt where he should have walked and spent six weeks below with a broken ankle. Louisa listened, but with averted looks; the moral was too plain.

***

The Harvilles' lodgings received them with a warmth and ingenuity which, even in disappointment, nobody could withstand. The rooms were small, close to the sea, and fitted up by Captain Harville's own hands into a hundred conveniences: shelves for curiosities, a stand for the children’s playthings, a net mended and hung to dry, a window secured against the winter gales with a contrivance of his own. Mrs. Harville, with a child upon her knee and another clinging to her gown, made room about the fire. Tea was brought. The wet shawls were taken to dry. The close air smelt of coal and bread and brine.

Louisa sat by the window, still cool. She answered Mrs. Harville politely, but her attention wandered to the rain beginning to strike the glass. Anne, seated opposite, observed the struggle between pique and good breeding, and felt for her with a sister's sort of indulgence, though she was no sister. To be nineteen, to be admired for spirit, and to be told before one's friends that spirit must yield, was a lesson which could not be learned in an afternoon.

Captain Benwick, in the corner, seemed to feel the constraint most. He had been silent upon the Cobb, and he was silent still, turning over the leaves of a volume of poetry without reading. Anne, from kindness, and from a wish to give the others time to settle, addressed him upon the book. It was Scott, and they spoke a little of the lady of the lake and of metre, until his shyness gave way to something like eagerness. He had a mind full of feeling, and wanted only a listener who would not laugh.

Wentworth, meanwhile, was talking to Harville by the fire, but his eyes were not quite upon his friend. Anne was sensible of being watched and of watching in return, though neither looked directly. When Mrs. Harville rose to fetch more tea, there was a shifting of seats, and Wentworth found himself upon the low stool near Anne's chair, with the children playing at his feet.

"You think me very inconsistent," he said abruptly, in a low voice meant for her alone. The child beside him was pulling at his coat button, and he detached the small fingers gently as he spoke. "You heard me yesterday. The nut, and all that nonsense about firmness. And to-day I preach caution. Miss Elliot must think me a pretty moralist."

Anne was taken by surprise, the more because he had so long avoided any conversation which required an answer from her. She kept her hands quiet in her lap.

"I think you were very right to-day," she said. "The steps were wet. It would have been — it might have ended very ill."

"It might," he said gravely. "I saw it, all at once, as she stood up there. Last night I talked as if obstinacy were a virtue. I meant — I meant spirits, resolution in a good cause. But a young lady might take it for leave to do anything. If she had slipped — " He stopped. The colour left his face and returned. "I should never have forgiven myself. Harville would not have let me forget it."

"But she did not slip," said Anne. "You prevented her. That is the end of it."

"She is angry with me," he said, glancing towards the window. "And perhaps justly. I encouraged her to value herself upon never being persuaded. What right have I to complain if she will not be persuaded by me?"

There was a bitterness in the last words which Anne could not mistake, though others might have taken it for pleasantry. She understood that he spoke not only of Louisa upon the Cobb, but of an older persuasion, an older firmness once wanting where he had thought it due. Her heart beat uncomfortably, and she looked down at the child's head leaning against Wentworth's knee.

"To be persuaded and to be convinced are very different," she said, after a moment. "There are cases where yielding is weakness, and cases where it is duty. A friend who points out danger does not ask for blind compliance. Miss Louisa will see to-morrow that you did her a kindness."

He was silent. The little Harville boy had got his finger entangled in a knot of the fishing-net and set up a wail; Wentworth lifted him upon his knee with ready tenderness and freed the finger, kissing the red mark as a father might have done. The ease of the action, after the gravity of his words, moved Anne more than she could have expressed. She thought of Mrs. Musgrove's heavy grief for a worthless son, and of this man's capacity for affection towards everything helpless that came in his way.

Across the room, Charles Musgrove was describing the Cobb to Mrs. Harville, with exaggerations of Louisa's danger now that the danger was past. "She would have jumped as sure as fate if Frederick had not stopped her. He was as steady as a rock. I never saw him so serious." Louisa heard her name and turned her head. For an instant her eyes met Wentworth's over the child's fair hair. She looked away first, and bent to stroke the dog at her feet with unnecessary attention.

Tea was done. The rain increased. It was settled that the Uppercross party should remain the night at the inn, and that the Harvilles would keep Captain Benwick to supper. Cloaks were called for. In the bustle of leave-taking, Wentworth shook hands with Louisa with more than common warmth.

"We are friends?" he said. "You will not remember the Cobb against me?"

Louisa tried to smile. "Oh! I suppose I must forgive you. Though I dare say Henrietta thinks you used me ill."

"Henrietta may think what she pleases," said Wentworth, laughing, "so long as you acquit me. I would rather see you angry than hurt. That is a selfish doctrine, but a sailor's."

She let him press her hand, and the cloud lifted a little, but not wholly. As they crowded into the narrow passage, Anne heard Louisa whisper to her sister, "He treats me like a child now. Yesterday I was everything that was resolute." The words, though meant to be private, reached Anne with painful clearness, and she carried them with her into the rainy street.

***

The inn parlour that evening was close and noisy, with travellers coming in from the Exeter road and the smell of wet wool drying by the kitchen fire. The party supped early. Mary declared herself fatigued to death and full of apprehensions of a cold; Charles was in high good humour at having done the journey so well; the two girls, sharing a room above, dressed each other's hair and recovered their spirits in the manner of youth, which cannot long endure a check when health and novelty are on its side.

After supper, while Mary lay upon the sofa and Charles read the newspaper, Anne stood a while at the window, watching the rain run down the panes and listening to the sea. The events of the day arranged themselves in her mind with a distinctness she could not dismiss. She reviewed Wentworth's refusal, his paleness afterwards, his confession by Harville's fire. She reviewed Louisa's mortification, and the whisper in the passage. She asked herself, with a precision which cost her an effort, what she had hoped and what she had feared when Louisa stood upon the steps.

She had feared a fall; that was certain. She had feared the sight of a lifeless figure, the cries, the sending for a surgeon, the dreadful responsibility laid upon them all in a strange town. That fear being removed, what remained? A heaviness which she was unwilling to name. While Louisa was in danger of attaching Wentworth by her fearlessness, Anne had pitied her and admired her. Now that Wentworth had checked her, and Louisa was piqued, Anne pitied them both, and knew not what to wish. If his admiration survived the check, it would prove itself better founded than she had supposed. If it did not, what became of the attentions of the last month?

Her reflections were broken by Wentworth and Benwick coming in from the Harvilles', shaking rain from their hats. They had escorted Harville home and stayed for a glass of grog. Benwick soon withdrew to write a letter. Wentworth, finding no seat free but the chair opposite Mary’s sofa, took it, and fell into the idle talk of the evening: the state of the roads to Uppercross, the chance of getting horses in the morning, the folly of winter excursions to the sea.

Mary, revived by company, began upon Lyme and its delights, and upon the particular obligation they were under to Captain Wentworth for his care of Louisa. "I am sure," she said, "if Louisa had jumped, she must have been killed. I should never have got over it. Charles would have been inconsolable. And you so resolute, Captain Wentworth, that I quite stared. I thought you would indulge her in anything."

"I indulge nobody in breaking their necks, ma’am," said Wentworth, with a smile which did not reach his eyes. "Miss Louisa will thank me when she is cooler. Or she will not, and no matter." He turned the newspaper, then laid it down again. "Miss Elliot," he said, addressing Anne directly for the first time that evening, "do you think Lyme will gain or lose by our adventure? Shall we go home and report the Cobb dangerous, and frighten all Somersetshire from attempting it?"

Anne smiled. "I think we may report it beautiful, and advise care. That will not frighten anybody from coming who wishes to come."

"Care," he repeated. "Yes. Care is a dull counsellor, but it keeps one from some regrets. I have been too careless of counsel myself to recommend carelessness to others." He spoke lightly, but Anne heard the earnestness underneath, and Charles, looking up from his paper, laughed.

"Frederick moralizing! That is new. Next we shall have you writing sermons with Benwick."

"Benwick would write the better sermon," said Wentworth. "I can only practise when the danger stares me in the face." He rose, restless, and went to the window where Anne stood. The rain had eased. The street below shone black. For a minute they stood side by side, not speaking, while Mary’s voice ran on behind them about colds and damp sheets and the hardship of being obliged to sleep from home.

"You return to Uppercross to-morrow," he said at last, low. "And I to my brother’s, I believe. This party breaks up." Anne assented. "I am glad," he added, after another pause, "that to-day ended as it did. When I think what a few seconds might have made of it — a slip, a cry — and I standing with my hands out to receive what I ought to have forbidden — I am sick at the folly. You were the only one who did not press me to let her have her way. I thank you for that silence."

Anne could not answer immediately. To be singled out, after weeks of studied indifference, for such a confidence, overset her composure. She managed to say that she had been frightened, like the rest, and glad to be spared the consequence.

"Spared," he said. "Yes." He looked out into the darkness, where a lantern moved past towards the harbour. "Miss Louisa is young and lively, and I have done her an injustice by praising what I had no business to praise in the way I did. She desired only to please. It is I who set her upon pleasing by defiance. A man of thirty should know better."

Before Anne could reply, Louisa herself came down the stairs, fresh in a white gown hastily pressed for the evening, her hair curled, her smiles restored. She went straight to Wentworth and reproached him gaily for hiding in the window.

"Come and be agreeable," she said, taking his arm without ceremony. "Henrietta and I have agreed to forgive Lyme its rain if you will sing us that song about the sailor's return. Captain Benwick promises to join. You must not spend the evening in lectures."

Wentworth suffered himself to be led to the pianoforte which stood in the corner of the parlour. The little company gathered. His voice, a fine tenor a little roughened by the wind, rose above Benwick's lower tones. Anne sat apart with her work, listening, and watching Louisa turn the pages for him with recovered gaiety. The danger was past; the evening closed in comfort. Yet Anne carried away, as she retired for the night, the image not of the singing group, but of an earlier instant upon the Cobb: Wentworth standing below the steps with his hand extended, not to catch, but to guide; Louisa hesitating upon the wet stone; and the grey sea beating beyond. It seemed to her that something had been decided there besides the safety of an afternoon, though what, or for whom, she dared not yet determine.

The table under the tree was larger than any tea-table Alice had ever sat down to, and more crowded than any she had ever seen set, for the March Hare and the Hatter had spread themselves along nearly the whole of one side with their elbows among the cups, and the Dormouse sat wedged fast between them with his head nodding over a plate, while used cups and saucers stood three and four deep, with a milk-jug overturned upon its side and bread-and-butter laid in untidy piles wherever there was room to lay it; the afternoon sun came slanting through the leaves and laid bright patches upon the cloth, and the house behind them, with its chimneys like a pair of long ears and its roof thatched all over with fur, stared down at the feast as if it were accustomed to it. Alice herself was squeezed at one corner with her frock hitched clear of a sticky saucer and her feet tucked under the leg of her chair, for there was very little room to spare, and she was already wishing that she had not been quite so ready to take the place that was *not* offered her; she had come to the table meaning to rest a moment and to be civil, and now she found herself answering questions she had not been asked and defending manners she had never been taught to doubt, which, as she told herself, was not at all the proper way to take tea.

"You might at least offer a riddle that has an answer," said Alice, for the Hatter had just proposed a sort of question about a black bird and a desk for writing upon, and had seemed very much pleased with himself for having thought of it, though when she asked him to explain the likeness he had only grinned and tapped his great hat and said that she must guess it if she could.

"She wants an answer to everything," said the March Hare to the Hatter, as if Alice were not sitting close enough to hear him, which she was; "it is the fault of lessons; they put answers into children before the questions are ripe." And he pushed a cup toward her that had no tea in it, only a dark ring at the bottom where tea had once been, and said, "Drink, and do not argue."

Alice disputes with Hatter and March Hare at the large crowded outdoor tea-table, and indeed she could not help it, for the more she tried to be polite the more they turned her own words back upon her; when she said that she believed a riddle ought to mean something, the Hatter cried that meaning was a thing for dictionaries and not for tea, and when she said that it was not civil to press empty cups upon visitors, the March Hare corrected her at once and said that it was *she* who was uncivil for expecting a full one. "You do not understand clean cups," said the Hatter, leaning across the Dormouse, who squeaked faintly at being leaned upon, "we have done with washing; we move round when the things grow sticky. Time will not allow us to wash, and Time will not allow us to rest, and it is all on account of a certain great lady who would not hear a song out to the end." He looked so cross and so unhappy as he said it that Alice felt a moment of pity for him, though she was still vexed; "if Time will not help you," she said, "you might at least help one another to a little good manners."

"You should not talk at all if you cannot think to the purpose," said the Hatter very rudely, and he turned his back upon her so far as the crowded bench would allow, and began to hum a scrap of tune through his nose as if the conversation were finished.

That was more than Alice had bargained for, and she felt her face grow hot all the way to her ears; she was tired of being told that she was wrong when she knew she was right, and tired of bread-and-butter that nobody ate and tea that was never poured, and, as will happen with children who have been kept too long from their own size and their own supper, she began to feel that *somebody* ought to be appealed to. Without quite knowing what she meant to do she thrust her hand into the pocket of her frock, where she kept the two uneven crumbs of mushroom wrapped in a bit of paper, and her fingers met something hard and smooth that was neither crumb nor paper; it was a small flat case of black polished wood with brass corners, no bigger than a card-case, with a tiny crank at one side and a little bell upon the lid and a round mouthpiece folded down like the ear of a sleeping puppy. She had carried it about with her ever since the morning upon the bank (for what little girl, you know, will go out without her pockets full?), and had quite forgotten it among the bottles and keys and growing and shrinking; but now the sight of the brass crank gave her an idea so large that it seemed for a moment to fill the whole tea-table.

Alice displays a small black pocket telephone to Hatter and March Hare at the tea-table, holding it up between finger and thumb that they might see the bell catch the sun. "What is that?" said the March Hare, forgetting his rudeness in curiosity, and stretching his long ears forward until one of them dipped in the milk-jug; "it is not to eat, and it is not to drink, and therefore it has no business at tea." The Hatter left off humming and stared with his pale eyes very wide. "It looks like a snuff-box that has taken to machinery," said he. The Dormouse, who had been half asleep, opened one eye and murmured that bells were for ringing and ought not to be whispered about, and then shut his eye again.

"It is a pocket telephone," said Alice, with as much dignity as she could manage while squeezed against a teapot, "and it will carry my voice along a wire to any person I name, however far off they may be, and bring back theirs to me. You have only to turn the crank so, and to speak into this part, and to hold this other part to the ear. My sister says they are to be common one day, and that even cottages will talk to cottages." She unfolded the mouthpiece with great care, and a fine black cord, thin as sewing silk but strong as twine, came slipping out of the case and ran down over the tablecloth and across the grass, farther than the eye could follow among the roots and daisies; where the wire ended Alice could not tell, for it seemed to go on unwinding of itself, as threads do in dreams, growing longer the more one pulls.

The Hatter grew paler than before, if that were possible, and his great hat seemed to sit higher upon his untidy hair. "Put it away," said he quickly. "There are persons who ought not to be troubled at tea-time, and questions that ought not to be asked over wires. Time has troubles enough without telephones." But Alice, who was now quite resolved, and a little out of patience, as honest children will own to being when they have been contradicted for half an hour, shook her head. "Time is exactly what I mean to ask about," said she. "You say a great lady spoilt your music and quarrelled with Time itself, and left you for ever at six o'clock; very well, then, I shall ask the lady herself whether it is true, and whether she means you to go without clean cups for ever. I shall ring up the Queen of Hearts."

At the name of the Queen the March Hare dropped the cup he was holding, which fortunately was empty, and the Hatter made a sort of clutch at the little black case as if to push it back into Alice's pocket. "You must not!" cried he. "You do not know her! She has no notion of music! She stamped and she shouted when I sang last, and since that day Time will not do a stroke for me! If she hears my voice upon the wire she will know me again, and then — and then —" He did not finish, for it is not pleasant to finish such sentences at tea. "Nonsense," said Alice, though her heart beat rather fast at her own boldness; "if she is a Queen she must be accustomed to being spoken to, and I mean to speak very politely indeed. Please do not jog my elbow."

Alice speaks into the pocket telephone at the tea-table beside Hatter and March Hare, having first turned the crank three times, which made the little bell give a thin impudent tinkle, like a farthing bell at a toy shop. She pressed the round ear-part to her ear and bent her mouth to the mouthpiece, and for a moment there was nothing but a faint crackling, as of dry leaves walking about inside the wood, and then a distant humming and a click, as if many little doors had opened and shut along the wire. "Please," said Alice, very distinctly, for she remembered that one should always be distinct upon instruments, "please will you give me the Queen of Hearts?" The March Hare held his breath and stared, the Hatter covered his face with his hands but peeped through his fingers, and even the Dormouse sat up and listened, with tea dripping from his whiskers.

There was a pause — a pause in which Alice could hear her own breathing against the polished wood — and then, quite suddenly and quite clearly, as if the speaker stood just behind the teapot, came a sharp, short voice that made them all jump. "Who presumes?" said the voice. "Who dares to pull my wire at this hour? Speak your name and your business, and be quick about it!" It was a woman's voice, high and commanding, and accustomed, as Alice perceived at once, to being obeyed before it had finished speaking; you might have known it for a royal voice, she thought afterwards, by the manner in which it expected the ear to come to it, instead of going to the ear.

Alice swallowed, and then spoke up as bravely as she could, for she felt that to hesitate now would be worse than to have never rung at all. "If you please, your Majesty," said she, "I am Alice, and I am taking — that is, I am sitting at — tea with the Hatter and the March Hare, and they say that Time has left them at six o'clock ever since your Majesty's concert, and that they can never have clean cups any more, and I thought it only fair to ask whether your Majesty meant it to go on." There was a sound upon the wire as of something heavy being set down with a crash, and then the voice came back louder than before. "Tea?" cried the voice. "At six o'clock? With *that* singer? Let me hear him speak! Put him to the instrument this instant!"

"I am not here!" cried the Hatter before he could stop himself, in a voice so shrill with fright that it must have run the whole length of the wire without any telephone at all; "I am nowhere! I am taking no tea! I am —" He clapped both hands over his mouth too late, and looked at Alice with eyes of absolute horror, as a mouse might look who had just announced himself to the cat. From the ear-part, held now a little way from Alice's ear that all might catch the dreadful words, came a roar that rattled the little bell upon the lid. "I know that voice!" cried the Queen of Hearts. "I know that murderer of tunes! Hold the wire fast! Do not dare to cut it! I am coming myself!"

Hatter dives beneath the large crowded outdoor tea-table beside Alice and March Hare, and indeed he lost no time about it, for the cloth was lifted in a great billow and his coat-tails vanished under the edge with a scuffle of shoes among the chair-legs and a rattle of spoons; a cup went over and soaked a heap of bread-and-butter, the milk-jug rolled but did not break, and presently his pale face appeared again, low down between Alice's boots and the March Hare's chair, peering out like a rabbit from a burrow. "Ring off! Ring off!" he whispered hoarsely, tugging at Alice's skirt with trembling fingers. "Say you were mistaken! Say it was a wrong number! Say anything!" The March Hare, who was torn between terror of the Queen and a sort of loyalty to his fellow at tea, bent down and whispered too. "Say we are gone out," said he. "Say the table is empty. Say Time has stopped and we are not here to stop with it."

But it was too late to say anything of the sort, for the black cord that ran from Alice's telephone had suddenly grown tight and straight, as if some strong hand had taken hold of it far away among the trees, and was following it hand over hand toward the table; Alice could feel the little case tugging in her lap, and she held it fast with both hands lest it should be pulled away altogether. "Oh!" she cried, half to herself and half to the others, "she is *coming* along the wire!" And so, you see, she was; for what is the use of a telephone wire, in Wonderland or out of it, if it will not show the way to the person who is speaking?

The wire grew tauter and tauter.

First they heard a trampling through the dry grass beyond the thicket, and then a rustling and a panting, and then the sound of short, angry footsteps that would not wait for brambles; the cord cut a straight dark line across the daisies and over the roots, quivering with haste, and presently, where the path turned by the rose-bushes, there burst into view a procession so out of breath and out of order that Alice could hardly believe her eyes. There were two soldiers shaped like playing cards, red hearts painted upon their backs, each holding a coil of the black cord as if it were a rope, and between them, with her crown pushed crooked over one ear and her cheeks the colour of sealing-wax, marched a short, stout, furious lady in a gown patterned all over with hearts, carrying a sceptre that she used as a walking-stick to beat the bushes aside. Behind them trotted the White Rabbit in his waistcoat, with his watch in one hand and his trumpet tucked under his arm, crying, "Your Majesty! Your Majesty! Pray take care of the roots!" in the most distracted manner, but the Queen paid no more heed to him than to the daisies she trod upon.

Queen of Hearts confronts Alice, Hatter and March Hare at the crowded tea-table, planting herself squarely before the cloth with her feet well apart and her sceptre pointed, while the card soldiers dropped the wire and stood at attention, and the White Rabbit hid himself behind the teapot and pretended to be consulting his watch. For a full half minute no one spoke; the sun winked upon the cups, the Dormouse slid slowly off his chair and concealed himself in the sugar-basin, and the March Hare stood up so hastily that he upset his own chair backwards upon the grass. The Queen's eyes were small and bright and round, and they moved from Alice, who still held the telephone in her lap, to the March Hare, who bowed so low that his ears swept the crumbs, and then down, under the edge of the cloth, to the pale face of the Hatter peeping out between the boots. "There!" cried she, stamping till the spoons jumped. "There is the wretch who bawled at my concert! Seize him by the heels and bring him out!"

"If you please, your Majesty!" cried Alice, and she slipped from her chair and set herself down upon the grass in front of the cloth, with her skirt spread wide over the place where the Hatter crouched; she did not quite know why she did it, except that it had been *she* who rang the bell and *she* who had brought this storm upon tea, and that it seemed cowardly to leave the others to face it alone. The Hatter's cold fingers clutched at the hem of her frock from underneath, and she could feel him trembling through the muslin, as a little dog trembles in thunder; the March Hare, who had expected to be ordered away, stared at her with his mouth open, and even the White Rabbit peeped from behind the teapot with an expression of mingled admiration and alarm. "He did not mean any harm by his singing," said Alice quickly, "and he has been punished enough by having always to take tea with no clean cups; besides, your Majesty, it was I who called you along the wire, and if anybody is to be scolded it ought to be me."

Alice shelters Hatter from Queen of Hearts beside March Hare at the tea-table, kneeling straight with her arms spread a little, as nurses spread their arms to keep chickens from the road, while the Hatter pressed closer under the shadow of her petticoat and the March Hare edged nearer to her elbow, whether to hide or to help she could not tell. The Queen's face grew redder than ever, if that were possible, and for a moment Alice thought she would burst out with one of those short commands that Queens in this country are so fond of; indeed the soldiers lifted their pikes a little way, and the White Rabbit whispered, "Your Majesty, the heads — shall I make a note of the heads?" in a tone that suggested he very much hoped she would say no. "Silence!" cried the Queen, but whether to the Rabbit or to them all Alice could not be sure. "You are a child, and children must be taught! Do you dare to stand between me and my justice?"

"I dare to stand between you and a person who is frightened," said Alice, and though her voice shook a little she looked the Queen full in the face, for she was growing angry herself now, as well as frightened, which, as you know, makes a great difference to the courage. "You have not heard any evidence, and you have not asked what song it was, and you cannot settle about Time by shouting along a wire. If Time is angry, you should beg his pardon as well as the Hatter." The March Hare gave a faint squeak at this boldness, and the Hatter uttered a muffled groan from beneath the cloth, as if he thought all was lost; but the Queen stopped short with her mouth open, for no one, it seemed, had ever told her to beg pardon of anybody, and she did not at all know how to begin.

It was the telephone that saved them from what must have come next, for just as the Queen lifted her sceptre to point once more at the trembling heap under the tablecloth, the little bell upon the lid, which Alice still held tight in one hand, began to ring again of itself, thin and impudent and quite uncalled for — *trring! trring!* — as if somebody else, somewhere along that endless wire, wished to speak to somebody. The soldiers lowered their pikes to stare, the White Rabbit dropped his watch into the milk-jug, and even the Queen paused with her arm in the air. Alice stared down at the vibrating case, and felt the cord jerk in her lap like a living thing; she had rung up a Queen, and a Queen had come, wire and all, to tea, and now the wire wanted something more of *her*. She looked from the bell to the pale eyes under the cloth and then to the furious lady with the crooked crown, and she understood, with a sinking of her heart that was quite new to Wonderland, that a voice once sent along a wire may travel farther than ever was intended, and may bring more company than ever was invited.
