The rain had laboured against my casement through all the latter hours of the evening, and my candle, which flickered among the vessels and irons wherewith I had pursued my unhallowed labour, had sunk to a short and guttering stump before I summoned the remnant of my resolution to bestow the final impulse upon those limbs extended before me. O what a night of mingled ardour and dread was that November night; for two years I had withheld myself from rest, from society, from the fair intercourse of nature, that I might arrive at this consummation, and now my hands trembled as they moved among the instruments, and my heart knocked against my ribs with a violence which seemed to rebuke the very stillness of the hour. Victor Frankenstein and the creature confront each other in the dark rainy midnight Ingolstadt workshop; for as the last tremor of being passed along those vast members, the lids, which I had fashioned with such presumptuous care for beauty, lifted from off a pair of sallow and watery orbs, the broad breast heaved with a deep and difficult respiration, and a convulsive agitation ran through the whole frame as a lake is troubled by a sudden wind.

How shall I delineate the aspect which then met my sight, or convey to any other bosom the tempest of horror and disappointment which overthrew all my former exultation. I had selected each feature as fair in itself, deeming that proportion upon a gigantic scale must produce a correspondent grandeur; yet the skin, of a yellow and parchment hue, clung too closely about the muscles and the courses of the arteries beneath, the hair hung black and lustrous to the shoulders, the teeth shone with a whiteness almost dazzling, and these luxuriances, which in a living man might have commanded admiration, served only to render more appalling the contrast with those clouded eyes set in hollows of dun white, with that shrivelled visage and those straight and colourless lips which now writhed in the first struggle of vitality. The beauty of my dream, for which I had sacrificed health and sleep and the communion of my beloved friends, vanished in that instant as a vapour before a storm; breathless loathing filled my heart, and I stood riveted, unable to endure the gaze of the being to whom I had imparted existence, yet unable, in that first stupor of creation, to withdraw my own.

I retreated at length into my bed-chamber, which adjoined the workshop by a narrow passage, and there traversed the floor for many minutes in an agony which no language can render; sometimes my pulse beat with such rapidity that I felt each artery throb as though it would burst its confines, and anon a languor seized upon my limbs so that I was fain to lean against the wainscot lest I should sink to the ground. Dreams that had nourished me through months of seclusion were now turned to bitterness, and I accused my own ardour, my impious curiosity, my neglect of every duty which ought to have restrained me. At last weariness so far mastered tumult that I cast myself, still clothed as I was, upon the bed, and sought in slumber a brief forgetfulness of that animated mass which breathed and moved within a few paces of my pillow. You who have known the fever of protracted study will comprehend how unquiet was the repose I courted; yet exhaustion closed my lids, and I passed into visions more terrible than waking.

Methought I beheld Elizabeth Lavenza advancing toward me through the streets of this foreign town with all the bloom of health renewed upon her countenance; delighted and transported, I hastened to enfold her, and imprinted a kiss upon those lips which I had so often in absence recalled with fraternal tenderness. But even as I embraced her, the warmth fled from her features, her lips assumed the livid pallor of the grave, her golden tresses seemed to darken and to dampen, and I discovered that I sustained in my arms no living maiden but the corpse of my departed mother, wrapt in a shroud whose folds appeared to stir with the movements of the worm. I started from this phantasm with a cry half smothered in my throat; a cold dew stood upon my forehead, my teeth smote together, every joint was convulsed with terror, when, by the dim and sallow light of the moon forcing itself betwixt the shutters, I perceived the curtains of my bed drawn slowly aside by an immense and yellow hand. There stood the wretch whom I had animated; his eyes, if those watery apertures may be so denominated, were fixed earnestly upon my face, his huge jaws parted, and from them issued low and broken sounds devoid of articulation, while a grin, occasioned rather by the unpractised contraction of new muscles than by any sentiment of derision, wrinkled his cheeks. One arm, vast and discoloured, was extended toward me, as though to detain or to implore, and the whole towering figure inclined forward in an attitude of supplication and of wonder.

My first and most violent impulse was to fly; to cast myself down the staircase, to take refuge through the night in the open courtyard below, to place bolts and distance betwixt myself and this horrid product of my art, and never again to behold those features which accused me. The blood rushed to my heart and then receded, leaving me faint; my limbs already gathered themselves for flight, and my eye sought the door. Yet in that very instant there arose within me another and more imperious voice, which neither fear nor disgust could wholly silence. Was not this solitary and shuddering thing my work, my offspring in a sense more dreadful than that of ordinary paternity, cast without knowledge or consent into a world where every countenance must affright him. Had I not, in bestowing life, assumed a charge which no subsequent horror could absolve; and should the creator abandon his creature at the first cry of its helplessness, as a coward deserts the vessel he has himself launched upon a tempestuous sea. O presumptuous and unfeeling man that I had been, to desire glory without burthen; and now, when the burthen stood before me and stretched forth its hand, should I prove myself at once cruel and base. Curiosity, too, that old and fatal spur of my nature, withheld me; for those inarticulate murmurs bespoke some inward operation of sense, some dawning desire to communicate, and I burned, even through my terror, to learn what thoughts already tenanted that capacious brow. I did not flee; I remained, though every nerve revolted, and compelled my failing limbs to sustain me upon the edge of the couch.

Victor Frankenstein and the creature touch hands in the narrow small moonlit shuttered Ingolstadt bedchamber; for seeing that his outstretched fingers caused me to shrink, he paused, and his vast countenance assumed an expression which I could interpret only as distress, and then, with a gentleness wholly unexpected from such ponderous limbs, he lowered his hand until the palm hung open and empty before me. The moon lay in pale bars across the coverlet, the rain still whispered without, and in that solemn stillness I slowly raised my own thin and trembling right hand and suffered it to rest for a moment within his. His skin was cold as the damp earth of a newly opened grave, yet it quivered beneath my touch as though the contact conveyed to him some strange and unwonted consolation; his fingers, of enormous length and power, closed not to crush but to retain, with a timid pressure which seemed to fear its own strength, and his breast emitted a deep and sighing sound, not of menace but of satisfaction, as a child that has long wept in darkness and at last finds a familiar presence. My flesh crept, I confess it, and my soul recoiled even as my hand remained; yet I endured, and looking steadfastly into those watery eyes, I perceived therein no malice, but only bewilderment and a piteous eagerness to be acknowledged.

I spoke, though my voice at first emerged hoarse and broken from my parched throat. "Be still," said I, endeavouring to modulate my tones as one might address a startled and suffering invalid, "be still; thou shalt receive no injury from me." The sound of human speech appeared to agitate him powerfully; he drew back his head, regarded my lips with fixed attention, and attempted, with painful contortions of mouth and throat, to imitate the cadence, producing only those same rude and plaintive murmurs. He presently sank, rather than sat, upon the floor beside my bed, his huge knees drawn upward, his shoulders bowed beneath the low ceiling, and there remained gazing alternately at my face and at his own extended limbs, as though comparing his state with mine and seeking in my demeanour some explanation of his existence. Pity, that tardy but irresistible visitant, began at length to contend in my bosom with horror; for I reflected that this being, however hideous in outward form, had committed no crime, had uttered no threat, had sought only, by such means as nature had afforded him, to express a want which every living soul must feel, the want of recognition by its maker.

The chill of the November night penetrated even through my chamber walls, and I observed that the naked shoulders of the creature, for I had provided no raiment proportioned to his stature, were mottled with cold, and that a slight and continual shivering passed along his frame. Victor Frankenstein cloaks the creature in the candlelit cluttered narrow stone vaulted upper Ingolstadt chamber; for rising with unsteady steps, I fetched from a press the largest travelling cloak which I possessed, a heavy garment of dark wool lined with coarse baize, and returning to where he couched, I cast it about those gigantic limbs. He started at first as the cloth descended, as though apprehending a blow, but feeling its warmth and weight, he drew it closer with his own hands, awkwardly and yet with evident gratitude, muffling his throat and breast as an infant might clutch at swaddling bands. I fastened the clasp as best I could beneath his chin, though my fingers trembled so violently that the task occupied many moments, and stood back to regard my work. Enveloped thus, his vast proportions seemed less a mockery of human shape and more the semblance of some benighted traveller overtaken by calamity; and though his visage retained its ghastliness, the act of clothing him, so simple and so domestic, softened in my own mind the extremity of my abhorrence, as though by performing toward him one office of humanity I had acknowledged a tie which could not henceforth be wholly severed.

***

Through the remainder of that dismal night I watched beside him, for I dared neither to sleep again nor to leave him unwatched lest ignorance should lead him into mischief. I brought him water in an ewer, which he received with both hands and drank with loud and untaught eagerness, spilling much upon the cloak; I offered him a portion of bread left from my supper, which he examined long, smelled, and at last devoured, uttering a low sound that bespoke contentment. Each action confirmed what my reason already suggested, that his senses were acute but uninstructed, his strength prodigious but as yet undirected by intention. When the candle guttered and threatened extinction, he shrank visibly from the encroaching darkness and crept nearer to the dying flame, extending his immense palms toward its warmth as toward a living friend; and when I trimmed the wick and the light revived, his countenance brightened with a delight so artless that I could not forbear a melancholy reflection upon the fate of Adam, who had awakened not among instruments and stone but amid the mild airs of Paradise, greeted by a benevolent voice. What voice had greeted my Adam. None but my own groan of execration, had I yielded to my first cowardice; and even now, what prospect could I unfold before him but obscurity and scorn. Yet I resolved, as I sat through those slow hours listening to the rain and to his heavy breathing, that I would not at least commence his history with desertion; I would endeavour to instruct his dawning faculties, to restrain his power by kindness, and to conceal him from the uncharitable gaze of men until I might determine what justice demanded both for him and for society. This resolution, I own, was mingled with selfish apprehension; for who would credit my tale if he were discovered, and what infamy or accusation of madness might not fall upon me.

Morning, dismal and wet, at length dawned, and discovered through my rain-streaked panes the white steeple of the church with its clock pointing to the sixth hour. The porter below unbarred the gates of the courtyard which had so often afforded me passage to my solitary walks, and the sound of wheels upon the miry street recalled me to the ordinary duties of life which I had so long neglected. My guest, exhausted by the novel exertion of existence, had fallen into a profound slumber upon a heap of coats which I had arranged for him in the inner recess of my workshop, his vast breast rising and falling with regularity, his hand still clutching the edge of my cloak. Judging it unsafe to leave him wholly unsecured, yet perceiving the absolute necessity of air and of intelligence from without, I softly closed the inner door, turned the key upon him for the briefest interval, and issued forth with quick and irregular steps into the comfortless streets, hoping that bodily motion might allay the fever of my spirits and enable me to devise some permanent means of shelter for the being upstairs.

I had wandered without clear purpose toward the quarter where the public diligences discharge their passengers, when my eyes were arrested by the arrival of the Swiss coach, steaming and bespattered from its nocturnal journey. The door was opened, and among the travellers who alighted I discerned, with a transport which for a moment obliterated every darker thought, the familiar and beloved figure of Henry Clerval. "My dearest Henry!" I cried, hastening forward and seizing his hand with an ardour which surprised even myself, "what fortunate and unexpected providence hath conducted thee to Ingolstadt at this precise season of my need." He returned my embrace with his accustomed warmth, his handsome countenance glowing through fatigue, and declared that no welcome could exceed the joy of his arrival, for he had at length prevailed upon his father to permit him to pursue his studies beside me. The sight of one connected with my father, with Elizabeth Lavenza, with all those scenes of domestic affection at Belrive, restored to my thoughts a world from which I had long exiled myself; I grasped his arm and for a short space forgot my horror, experiencing for the first time in many months a sensation approaching to calm and serene joy.

As we walked together toward my college, Henry discoursed with animation upon our mutual friends and upon his own good fortune in obtaining leave to quit the counting-house for the land of knowledge; he described the health of my father, grown somewhat aged but still upright in his benevolence, the improving spirits of Elizabeth, who awaited my letters with affectionate impatience, and the welfare of my younger brothers, whose sports he painted with humorous fidelity. I inquired with eagerness after each particular, yet even while I listened my conscience smote me; for how could I, who harboured beneath my roof a secret so portentous, meet the clear eye of this ingenuous friend without dissimulation. Henry presently interrupted his narrative, stopping short in the miry lane and gazing full into my face. "My dear Frankenstein," said he, in tones of solicitude, "forgive my frankness, but thou appearest wretchedly ill; thou art thin and pale as one who hath watched for many nights, and thy eyes possess a wildness which alarms me. Confess truly, hast thou not overtasked thy constitution with study." I trembled excessively, for the inquiry touched too nearly upon truths I dared not utter; I assured him that my labours were now concluded and that liberty and his society would soon restore me, speaking with a precipitation which I fear betrayed rather than concealed my inward perturbation.

We arrived at length at the foot of the staircase leading to my apartments, and here my terror revived with redoubled force; for I recollected that the being whom I had left locked in slumber might have awakened, might have forced the imperfect fastening, and might even now be traversing my rooms in search of me. Dreading above all things that Henry should encounter him unprepared, I entreated my friend to remain for a few minutes below while I ascended to assure myself that my chambers were in fitting order to receive him. Henry laughed gently at my fastidiousness, but consented with his usual compliance, remarking that he would examine the notices affixed to the college gate. I darted upward, my hand already upon the lock before I recollected to compose my features; I paused, a cold shivering seized me, and I threw open the door as one who expects a spectre. What was my mingled relief and dismay to discover my guest awake and seated upon the heap of coats, the cloak still about his shoulders, his huge form bent attentively over the dying embers of my stove, which he appeared to be fostering with cautious breath. He turned at my entrance and uttered his low plaintive sound, extending his hand as before, and I hastened to enjoin silence by gestures, my heart palpitating with the knowledge that Henry waited only a few yards beneath.

My caution arrived too late; for Henry, grown impatient or apprehensive at my prolonged absence, had followed softly up the stone steps, and now stood upon the landing without. Henry Clerval recoils from the creature on the narrow sunlit stone steep Ingolstadt college staircase; for the door, which I had left ajar in my haste, afforded him a full view of the interior, where the vast and cloaked figure had risen at my approach and now towered in the grey morning light admitted through the unshuttered casement. Henry halted upon the worn step, his hand tightening convulsively upon the iron rail, his handsome features blanched to an ashen hue, his whole frame shrinking backward as though a precipice had opened before him. The creature, perceiving a stranger, uttered a louder and more agitated murmur and advanced a pace, not in menace but in that same eager curiosity wherewith he had regarded me; yet his stature, his sallow visage half concealed by the hood of my cloak, his immense hands protruding from the folds, presented an apparition which might have appalled the stoutest heart. The pale daylight streaming through the narrow stair window fell full upon them both, the one slight and graceful in his travelling coat, the other gigantic and shrouded, and for an instant neither moved.

Victor Frankenstein bars the doorway against pale Henry Clerval in the narrow crowded Ingolstadt lodgings; for recovering from my stupor, I cast myself between them, spreading my arms across the narrow frame and pressing my back firmly against the panels that I might prevent either entrance or further vision. "Retire, Henry, I conjure thee!" I exclaimed with a vehemence which astonished even myself, "advance not a step further upon thy life; this apartment containeth a pestilential vapour from my chemical pursuits which hath already disordered my own brain, and the unfortunate sufferer within is in a state which no eye should behold." My friend gazed at me in utter bewilderment, his alarm for my safety now contending with his horror at what he had seen. "My dear Victor, what delirium is this," he cried, endeavouring to peer past my shoulder, "what unhappy man hast thou concealed here, and why am I, thy oldest friend, forbidden to afford him succour. Suffer me at least to summon a physician, for thou thyself art evidently distempered." I maintained my post with desperate obstinacy, feeling the creature stirring uneasily behind me and fearing each moment lest he should speak or emerge; I pleaded fatigue, contagion, a chemical accident which had disfigured a poor assistant whom shame induced to hide himself, inventing falsehood after falsehood with a facility which afterwards filled me with remorse, yet preferring any guilt of equivocation to the disclosure of a truth which must brand me as either madman or sorcerer.

By earnest entreaty and by invoking the memory of our childhood friendship, I at length prevailed upon Henry to descend to the lower landing, exacting from him a solemn promise that he would for the present breathe no word of what he had glimpsed to porter or to professor. He yielded, though with evident reluctance and with many backward glances expressive of grief and suspicion; his compliance cost me more than any reproach could have done, for I perceived that I had planted betwixt us the first seed of distrust, and that his generous nature was already labouring to reconcile my strange demeanour with his affection. Having secured the outer door below, I returned to my apartments with a heart oppressed by the consciousness of deceit; yet necessity urged me onward, for the daylight increased, the house began to stir with servants and students, and discovery approached with every footfall upon the stairs. My guest regarded me with those questioning eyes which seemed hourly to acquire a deeper intelligence, and I comprehended that I could no longer detain him in a place exposed to perpetual intrusion.

Victor Frankenstein guides the creature through the empty grey wide rainy Ingolstadt courtyard at dawn; for drawing the hood of the cloak more closely about his head so as to shadow his unnatural features, and wrapping a second coarse covering about his shoulders to diminish his extraordinary bulk, I took him by the hand and led him by the least frequented passage toward the rear door which opened upon the courtyard. The rain fell steadily upon the uneven stones, the grey light revealed no loiterer beneath the arcade, and the porter, occupied with the morning diligence, had left the wicket unguarded. The creature followed with docile and heavy steps, stooping low to pass the lintel, his vast feet splashing in the puddles, his breath issuing in visible clouds upon the chill air. Once within the shelter of a ruinous wood-shed abutting the wall, where faggots and neglected implements afforded concealment, I enjoined him by signs to remain crouched and silent, placing my finger upon my lips in a gesture which he instantly and faithfully imitated. As I stood a moment regarding that huge and shrouded form huddled among the damp timber, while the rain beat upon the crazy roof above us, I felt the full and irrevocable weight of the charge I had assumed; I had preserved him from immediate desertion, but I had likewise bound myself to perpetual secrecy, to falsehood toward my dearest friend, to the dread of exposure, and to the arduous labour of humanising a being whom nature and man alike seemed disposed to abhor. Yet when he lifted his hand once more and timidly touched my sleeve, as though to assure himself that I would return, I found myself unable to renounce him, and departed to face Henry with a determination, however trembling, to instruct and to protect the wretched life I had called forth.

remixes.chapter:
The parlour was a small affair, and cold with that particular London cold which gets into the wainscot and sits there, and will not be coaxed out by a handful of coal; and yet the lamp upon the table burned with a steady yellow eye, and threw its light upon two figures who sat too far apart for lovers, though once they had sat close enough, Heaven knows! The young man had the sharp look of one who counts and counts again, even when there is nothing upon the table but a tea-cup and a folded letter; the girl wore a dark mourning frock, plain and brushed with a woman's care, and her hands lay folded in her lap as if to keep them from trembling. Oh, you who have sat in such a room, with the fire gone low and the street noises dulled by fog outside, you know the weight of the air when something long deferred must at last be spoken!

Scrooge, the old man, stood with the Ghost of Christmas Past a little apart from them, unseen and unheard as shadows among shadows; and his own sharp breath came short, for he knew this room, he knew the pattern of the paper, he knew the chipped edge of the mantel where he had once rested his elbow in confident youth. The Spirit's light fell from its crown in a clear jet, and shewed every threadbare place in the carpet, every polished patch upon the young man's coat, and the tears standing unfallen in Belle's eyes; and Scrooge put his hand to his own cheek, marvelling to find it dry when all within him felt drowned.

Belle spoke, and her voice was low and even, with that terrible gentleness which costs a woman more than anger. She told him, in her own soft and reasoned way, that another love had taken her place; not another woman, but a bright and hard affection which could be locked in an iron chest. She said they had been poor and content when they pledged themselves, and that poverty then had been a thing to be borne together; but now he feared the world's reproach, and laboured to stand beyond its sneer, and weighed every kindness as a merchant weighs sugar. Was she unjust? She asked it mildly, with steadiness, and would take no answer that was not true.

The young Scrooge answered with heat, as a man will when the truth has found the joint in his armour. What! Was it a crime to wish to be secure? Was the world so tender to poor men that he should court its pity? He had seen what came to clerks who married upon hope and lived upon air; he had added and subtracted, and the figures would not lie. Poverty, said he, is sharp and unmannerly, and the world condemns the man who seeks wealth even as it tramples the man who lacks it. There was justice, after a fashion, in his plea; and yet, even as he spoke, his eye went to the window where the fog pressed its dun face, and to the empty grate, as if reckoning the cost of another lump.

Belle rose, for she had said what she came to say, and her release was ready upon her lips; it trembled there, kind and final, the gift of a full heart to the lad he had been. She would free him, she said, and bear no malice; he might go his chosen road, and be happy in it if he could.

Then it befell — and here, reader, mark it well, for all that follows hangs upon this hinge — that young Scrooge did not bow his head and let her go, as pride counselled and as use and habit bade him. His face, which had begun to set into those eager and restless lines that gain loves to carve, broke all at once like ice upon a pond in thaw. He cried out her name as a drowning clerk might cry for a ledger-line to hold by, and Young Scrooge kneels toward Belle in the small cold bare lamplit upstairs London parlour. Down he went, knee to the worn carpet, his coat-tails in the dust, his hands outstretched and empty of papers for once in his counting life; the lamp threw his great shadow up the wall, where it shook and wavered. Think of it! A man who had learned to kneel to no creditor, kneeling to a dowerless girl in a hired room!

"Belle! Belle! Do not cast me off!" he cried, and the words tumbled from him thick and unpractised, for entreaty was a foreign tongue to him. "I am altered, I own it; I am grown fearful and griping, and the rust of figures is upon me. But stay — only stay — and I will mend. Marry me poor, marry me now, and I will prove that love can keep accounts with prudence. Do not leave me to become the thing you pity. I beg it of you upon my knees; I, who have begged nothing of any man!"

The Ghost of Christmas Past made no sign, though its light burned a shade the brighter; and old Scrooge, forgetting that he was a shadow, stretched his own withered hand as if to pluck his younger self upright, and whispered, "Rise, fool! Let her go in kindness!" But the shadows hear nothing, you know; they have no consciousness of us, and go their appointed way.

Belle stood above him, and her cheek was wet at last, and her folded hands had come unfolded. What woman could see such abasement unmoved, when she had loved the boy who now knelt in the man's stiff coat? She had come armed with reason, with every measured sentence laid in order like linen in a press; and reason melted. She thought of the long winter evenings she would have spent alone if she left him, and of his solitary lodgings, and of the hard master he served, and pity — that dangerous counsellor — pleaded louder than prudence. Slowly, as one who sets down a burden she knows she must lift again, she put her hands upon his shoulders.

"Ebenezer," she said softly, "if I stay, will you hold me dearer than profit?"

"Dearer than breath!" he swore, and meant it with his whole trembling soul; and Young Scrooge embraces Belle in the small cold bare long narrow lamplit upstairs London parlour. Up he sprang and caught her to him, lamp-light and tear-light mingling, her mourning frock crushed against his waistcoat, her braided hair loosened against his cheek; the little table rocked with the suddenness of it, and the tea-cup rang against the saucer like a tiny bell. It was no graceful wooing, Heaven forgive them! It was hungry and awkward and true, as the embraces of the poor are apt to be when they have pawned their pride for love. Old Scrooge sobbed aloud, and laughed in the same breath, and the Spirit regarded him with mild and searching eyes.

***

The church was old and cold enough to make a bride's fingers ache within her gloves, though the sun that December morning did its thin best through the high windows, and laid pale slabs of light upon the stone. There were no carriages at the door, no favours, no breakfast spread in a great house; only a clerk with a cough, and a cousin of Belle's in a dyed gown, and a fellow lodger who had been coaxed to stand as witness with the promise of a glass of negus afterwards. And yet — and yet! — Belle walked the short aisle with her head high, in her best bonnet trimmed anew with ribbon, and her step had the music which no organ can give. For love, when it is young and has just snatched victory from parting, wears a wedding-gown though it be only merino.

Young Scrooge waited in a coat brushed till the nap shone, his cravat tied with more care than he had ever given a balance-sheet; his hands, those counting hands, shook as he drew the plain gold ring from his waistcoat pocket, where it had rattled all night against a loose halfpenny. He had paid for the licence with money saved by supperless evenings, and had reckoned the rent of two small rooms to a shilling, and the coal to a scuttle; and still he smiled, for figures for once had served romance. The parson, a stout gentleman with a cold in his head, read briskly, being anxious for his dinner; the responses came faint and then firm.

Young Scrooge weds Belle in the bright sunlit small high cold ancient stone London church. He took her hand, and the ring, a little too large, slipped firm upon her finger; he bowed his head as the blessing fell, and she looked up through happy tears. The cousin sniffed audibly, the lodger trod upon the clerk's toes in his eagerness to see, and the pigeons rattled upon the roof without. It was done in a dozen minutes, as parish weddings are; and out they came into the frosty air, man and wife, with nothing in the world but health, and hope, and fifteen shillings a week precariously earned, and a love that had refused to be released. Old Scrooge, beholding it, clapped his hands like a boy at Fezziwig's ball, and cried, "Bless her! Bless me!" till the Spirit touched his arm for silence.

***

They lodged at first above a chandler's shop in a narrow street where the fog lay all day like a lodger that would not pay; two low rooms under the tiles, where a man must stoop beneath the beam and learn to be humble in more senses than one. Belle made them sweet with muslin curtains washed to snow, and a geranium in a cracked pot, and a hearth swept till the bricks shewed their colour; she cooked a mutton chop as if it were venison, and eked potatoes and tea into feasts, and sang while she mended his shirts by a farthing candle. For a season — ah, that brief season which landlords never allow long enough! — Scrooge came home early, and carried up the coals himself, and read aloud of Valentine and Orson to make her laugh, and was almost the Ebenezer of old Fezziwig's warehouse, aproned and merry.

But rent will not wait upon kisses, and coal-merchants are no collectors of sighs. Marley's office, where young Scrooge copied and fetched and ran, grew sterner as trade pinched; the master, one Jorkin of hungry reputation before Marley took the reins alone, docked wages for lateness and charged interest upon advances. Young Scrooge, now a husband, felt fear with a new edge; not for himself alone, but for the woman who trusted him and for the small life already stirring beneath her apron. He stayed late to earn a sixpence, and came home with ink upon his fingers and figures dancing before his eyes; he counted the week's housekeeping upon the corner of the table, and found it short, and counted again, as if repetition would breed pence.

Belle watched him, and her song died by degrees, as a fire dies when the coal is husbanded too closely. She did not reproach; she darned and waited, and put his supper to keep warm, and nursed her growing weariness in silence. One midnight, when the chandler's shutters were barred below and the street lay empty save for the watchman's rattle, he sat at the deal table with a tallow dip guttering beside him, casting up arrears and prospects, while she sat opposite with her mending fallen in her lap.

"See here, love," he said, with an eagerness that was half apology, half defence, "if I take the extra copying at fourpence the folio, and forgo the dinner hour, we clear the quarter's rent and have a shilling to the good. Figures are friends, Belle; they do not flatter, but they do not desert." And Young Scrooge lifts the heavy ledger before Belle in the low midnight attic lodgings. Up he held the great bound book he had borrowed from the office to practise fair hand, its leather scarred and its pages ruled in red, as a soldier might lift a shield; the candle-light struck upon his lean wrist and upon the columns of neat figures, and upon Belle's pale face beyond it. He meant it kindly, Heaven help him! He meant to shew her safety made visible, provision proved in black and white. But between his eyes and hers the ledger stood like a wall, and the shadow of its boards fell across her lap where her hands lay idle.

She smiled, for she loved him, and praised his industry; yet when he bent again to his sums, she looked long at the low ceiling and at the frost upon the inside of the panes, and her hand crept to her side where the child pressed. Old Scrooge groaned to see it, and turned to the Spirit. "I meant well!" he faltered. "Was it not my duty to labour for her?" The Ghost answered in its soft and distant voice, "Duty is a good servant and a hard master. Look on."

***

Years are swift couriers, though they trudge in hobnailed boots; they brought two children to the attic and then took the attic away, exchanging it for three damp rooms in a basement where the daylight came sideways through area railings and the pump froze in January. Belle was a matron now, comely still, but thin as a worn glove; her mourning frock had long been turned and turned again, and her hair, once braided so proudly for a lover's fingers, was gathered plainly beneath a cap. She kept the rooms clean as a pin, mind you! She boiled bones into broth that would have deceived a lord, and patched the children's pinafores with scraps that matched by miracle; but no thrift could conjure coal from the cellar when the merchant would not trust, nor medicine from the air when the little girl coughed through December nights.

Young Scrooge was no longer young except in years; care and avarice, those twin clerks, had entered his face and taken possession, ruling lines about his mouth and kindling a restless glitter in his eye. He was Marley's man now, confidential copyist, trusted to dun and to distrain; he did his work thoroughly, and was praised for it in words that never warmed. He brought home more money than of old, and less of himself; his talk was of bills overdue, of debtors who feigned illness, of the folly of giving time. He loved his wife — ah, do not doubt it, reader, for love does not die in a night! — but he loved her as a man loves a bond he cannot afford to forfeit, anxiously, and with a growing terror lest the interest swallow the principal.

That winter evening the kitchen fire was out, for coal was sixpence the hundredweight beyond their reckoning, and the children had been put to bed upstairs in their shawls to keep warm. A single dip burned upon the dresser, and threw long shadows from the pot-hooks and the empty kettle. Belle stood by the table, her hands resting upon its scrubbed top, and waited till her husband had hung his hat and drawn off his gloves finger by finger, as was his careful habit.

"Ebenezer," she said, and her tone was still soft, though weariness had thinned it, "the little one needs the doctor. Mrs. Dilber's lad had the same cough, and bark and syrup cured him. I ask no finery, no outing, only this."

He frowned, not from cruelty — mark that! — but from that sordid fear which had become his daily bread. "Doctors are dear, Belle. A guinea for a visit and a bottle. We owe the baker, and Marley presses for the quarter's accounts to balance to a farthing. Wait till pay-day; warmth and gruel will do."

"Warmth!" she echoed, glancing at the cold hearth. "We have husbanded warmth till it is gone." She drew a folded paper from her apron — his own neat account of the month, kept in his fairest hand — and laid her finger upon the total. "You labour early and late, and I honour you for it; but tell me truly, husband, what idol have we served? When I stayed, you swore I was dearer than profit. Am I? Are these?" She gestured toward the ceiling, where the children's thin cough sounded faintly through the boards.

He flushed, and his hand went to his pocket where his purse lay lean, and his answer came in figures, for figures were his fortress. Belle listened, and shook her head with that old steadiness, sadder now for use. Belle faces Young Scrooge in the bare cold fireless damp winter small basement London kitchen. Straight she stood before him across the narrow table, her shawl drawn close, her eyes meeting his without flinching; he fronted her with ledgers in his head and fear in his throat, a man besieged in his own house. The dip guttered, and the damp struck up through the flags, and the unlit grate yawned like a reproach. Neither touched the other; that was the pity of it. Once they had clung in a lamplit parlour; now a deal board, though but three feet wide, might have been the Thames in flood.

"I stayed because you begged me," she said at last, very quietly. "I do not repent my pity. But I will not see our babes grow thin to keep your books handsome. My cousin in Shields will take us till spring. Come to us when you can leave your figures long enough to be a father." He opened his mouth to protest of rent and ruin and the world's hard judgment; and she heard him out, for she was ever patient, and then turned to pack a small bundle, weeping without sound, as women weep who have no time for sobs. Old Scrooge cried out, "Belle! Stay! Bid him burn his ledgers!" and would have rushed between them, but the Spirit's gentle grasp held him as lightly and as firmly as a woman's hand.

***

The bedroom was dark and cold as a vault, with the bed-curtains drawn close and the gruel untouched upon the hob; the church clock somewhere beyond the fog was labouring toward one, and every timber of the old house seemed to listen. Old Scrooge lay half-recumbent, his nightcap awry, his dressing-gown clutched about him, staring at the Ghost of Christmas Past whose light no longer danced but burned with a fierce and sorrowful brightness. The visions of the basement kitchen still hung before his eyes; he could see Belle's bundle tied with string, and the children's small shoes, and his younger self standing with his purse in his hand while his wife went out into the sleet — not in anger, oh, reader! but in that quiet despair which is anger's elder and more terrible sister.

"Spirit!" he gasped, tossing upon the pillows. "She stayed! I prayed her to stay, and she stayed, and see what my love has done! Had she left me at first, she might have known comfort; had I let her go, I had been only lonely. Now I am guilty of her want, and of theirs! Take me back! Haunt me no longer! Shew me no more, for I cannot bear it!"

The Ghost regarded him mildly, and in its face there seemed fragments of all the faces it had shewn him — Fan's bright forgiveness, Fezziwig's jovial benevolence, Belle's young hope and Belle's worn patience — shifting and blending like clouds. "These are shadows of the things that have been," it said in its soft and far-off tone. "That they are what they are, do not blame me. You bade love tarry without bidding gain depart; and two masters will not lodge in one breast in peace."

Scrooge could bear no more of that clear light, for it shewed him not only what he had lost but what he had spoiled by keeping. With a sudden and desperate strength he seized the great extinguisher-cap that hung beneath the Spirit's arm — oh, the folly of mortal hands that think to put out truth by covering it! — and Scrooge presses the extinguisher over the Ghost of Christmas Past in the dark bedroom. Down he drove it with all his force, his knuckles white, his breath hissing through his teeth; the cap swallowed the white tunic and the holly branch and the summer flowers, and for an instant darkness seemed to conquer. But though he pressed till his arms shook, he could not hide the light, which streamed from beneath in an unbroken flood upon the floor, and ran in luminous rivers to the bed's foot, and painted Belle's young face and Belle's worn face upon the curtains in awful succession.

Exhausted, drowned in remorse and in a drowsiness he could no more resist than the tide, he loosed his hold and reeled; the room swam, the light swam, the chimes of the coming hour beat faintly upon his failing sense. He sank toward his pillows with Belle's last quiet words ringing in his waking sleep, and the Ghost's radiance still burning beneath its cover, waiting — waiting — for what the night had yet to bring.

I started from my sleep as one starts from a grave; for in my dream I had clasped Elizabeth in the streets of our native town, and her lips, when I would have kissed them, had taken the livid stain of mortality, and my mother, long since buried, seemed to lie folded in my arms with the damp of the sepulchre upon her garments. A cold sweat stood upon my brow; my limbs shook with that palsy which extreme terror leaves behind it; and the chamber, which I had left in utter darkness save for the expiring wick of my candle, was now filled with a sallow and doubtful light, for the moon had forced her ray through the interstices of my shutters and laid a pale bar across the floor. Oh, how vividly does that hour return upon me! I hear again the rain beating against the casement with a sullen and unceasing murmur; I behold again the instruments of my labour scattered in wild confusion about the table; and I feel again, as I then felt, that sickness of the soul which follows upon a deed whose magnitude is comprehended only when it can no longer be recalled.

The curtain of my bed was drawn aside by a hand of prodigious size and of a yellowish hue, through which the play of the muscles might be discerned as through a veil. There stood the being whom I had endued with life scarce an hour before; his stature, even thus stooping beneath the low ceiling of my sleeping room, exceeded all common measure, and his countenance, livid where the lamp had shewn it livid, appeared in that lunar gleam still more ghastly by contrast with his flowing black hair and his teeth of a whiteness almost unnatural. His eyes, of a dull and watery yellow, were fixed steadfastly upon my face; his vast mouth was half opened, and there issued from it a succession of low, broken, inarticulate utterances, such as an infant might form who essays speech and finds only breath. One arm was extended toward me, the fingers spread abroad; and whether to implore, to caress, or to detain, I knew not. Learn from me, ye who pursue knowledge as I then pursued it, how terrible is the moment when the thing desired stands before the mind disrobed of desire, and asks, by its mere existence, what thou wilt now do with it!

Every nerve in my frame counselled flight. My feet had already gathered themselves for that spring which would have borne me down the staircase and into the court, where the night air might have cooled my brow; my hand had already seized the coverlid as a shield against a contact which I loathed. Yet in that very instant there rose within me another voice, which I must call conscience, though it spoke then with the accent of my father when he reasoned with me upon some boyish cruelty toward a bird or an insect. Had I not, with infinite labour, collected these limbs, joined these fibres, watched over this frame through winter silence and summer heat, and called upon the heavens to witness the innocency of my purpose? Was this vast infant, who had committed no crime, to be abandoned upon the first hour of his nativity because his visage displeased the eye that formed it? The thought smote me with a shame more acute than my horror; and though my flesh shrank, I did not flee. I remained; I pressed my back against the pillow; I compelled my eyes to endure what they would fain have shunned. Great God! what a combat then agitated my bosom!

Victor Frankenstein kneels before the creature beside the moonlit bed in the Ingolstadt chamber.

It was not a posture assumed from devotion, but from that sudden failure of strength which seizes a man after long watching and fasting, when the spirits sink and the knees refuse their office. I had risen to cast myself from the bed, and my limbs betrayed me; I sank upon the boards beside that portentous form, so that our faces were for a moment upon a level, his enormous and untaught, mine haggard with toil and terror. The moon laid her cold hand upon us both. He uttered again that strange, plaintive murmur, and bent his head, as if he would examine more nearly the countenance of his maker. I perceived then, with a pang which no language can render, that his look contained no malice; it contained wonder, and a wild desire to be acknowledged. He stretched forth his hand anew, and his fingers, whose joints were still stiff with newness, hovered near my shoulder without daring to rest upon it. I did not strike the hand aside. I suffered it, though every fibre in me recoiled, to remain suspended in the air between us, as a pledge that I would not that night forsake him.

"What art thou?" I whispered, though I knew well what he was; and then, ashamed of a question which he could not answer, I altered my tone and spoke as one speaks to a child afflicted with deafness. "Be still. I will not leave thee. Be still." Whether any meaning passed from my voice into his understanding I cannot affirm; but the agitation of his chest subsided by degrees, and the convulsive motion which had hitherto shaken his limbs gave place to a tremor less violent. The night was bitter, for November had breathed her frost upon Ingolstadt, and the rain which still fell without had chilled the apartment despite the dying embers in my stove. He was naked, save for some loose covering which I had thrown over his loins when first he breathed; and I beheld his skin, of that dun yellow which scarcely veiled the work beneath, contracted with cold, and his shoulders drawn together like those of a traveller unsheltered upon an Alp. My own teeth chattered, less from the air than from the fever of my spirits; yet pity, that late and reluctant guest, began to contend in my breast with disgust.

I rose, unsteady as a convalescent, and taking from a peg the heavy cloak in which I was accustomed to walk to my lectures, I advanced toward him. He watched my approach with eyes that followed every motion, as a dog follows the motion of a master whose temper he has not yet proved. When I lifted the garment, he shrank, fearing, as I suppose, some blow; but when I laid it gently about his vast shoulders and drew its folds across his breast, a sound escaped him, neither a groan nor a sigh, but something between the two, expressive of relief comprehended by the body before the mind has mastered it. Victor Frankenstein wraps a cloak around the shivering creature in the candlelit Ingolstadt workshop. The candle, which I then rekindled, cast its trembling yellow upon his countenance, and I marked how the light softened, though it could not beautify, those features which I had once selected for their imagined symmetry; his brow, so high and prominent, his lips, so straight and dark, his hair, so lustrous and abundant, formed indeed a whole which art might have admired in marble but which nature abhorred in life. Still, enveloped thus, seated upon the low stool beside my furnace, he appeared less a dæmon than a wretched outcast surprised by charity; and I, standing over him with the candle in my hand, felt for the first time since my labour began something like the gravity of a parent who perceives that his offspring must henceforth be a burthen as well as a charge.

What was to be done with such a charge in a university town, where every lodger is observed, every stranger remarked, every irregularity reported to the police? I had no plan; I had only the obstinate resolution that I would not repeat the cowardice of abandonment which my heart had already condemned. I bethought me of food, for I reasoned, with a natural philosophy more humane than that which had hitherto occupied me, that hunger must already torment a frame so vast and so newly animated. Upon my table lay the remains of my evening meal, a loaf of coarse rye, a portion of cheese, and a pitcher of milk now grown cold. I placed them before him, and with slow gestures, as one instructs a foreigner ignorant of our customs, I broke the bread and conveyed a morsel to my own mouth. He imitated the motion with an eagerness that alarmed me, seizing the loaf in his immense hand and crushing more than he conveyed. Victor Frankenstein watches the creature taste bread at the long wooden Ingolstadt chamber table. The crumbs fell upon his cloak and upon the floor; the milk ran down his chin; yet his eyes, as he ate, never quitted my face, seeking therein, as I divined, some confirmation that he had done well. I nodded, and uttered words of encouragement, though my voice sounded hollow in my own ears. He seemed to gather confidence from the tone, if not from the sense, and ate with less violence, attempting even, after several failures, to break the bread with moderation. Oh, strange and piteous school! I, who had aspired to penetrate the origin of life, was now reduced to teach its meanest necessity; and he, who had opened his eyes upon a world of learning, knew not yet how to satisfy his appetite without waste.

The hours which followed belong rather to the history of a mind than to that of outward events, and yet how deeply they are engraven upon my memory. I endeavoured, by repetition, to fix in his recollection the names of the objects about us; fire, bread, water, hand, eye; pronouncing each distinctly and pointing thereto, as my mother had once, as I have been told, instructed my infant lips. He listened with an attention painful in its intensity; his vast brow contracted with effort; his mouth laboured to shape sounds for which his organs, though perfect, possessed no habit. At times he succeeded in producing a rude approximation which transported me with a joy as disproportionate as my former despair; at times he failed, and uttered only that mournful bleat which reminded me how wide is the interval between sensation and speech. Was I then satisfied? No; for with every proof of his docility there returned upon me the consciousness of what I had wrought. His form, when he rose to fetch wood at my bidding and bore a burthen which three men could scarce have lifted, displayed a power that might one day become terrible; his countenance, when clouded by perplexity, assumed an expression which my fancy readily interpreted as sullen. Like our first parent, as Milton hath feigned him, he came forth innocent, yet already marked by a grandeur that separated him from common men; like the fallen angel, he might learn to curse the day that gave him being if that being yielded him only solitude. These thoughts oppressed me, even while I instructed him; and I marvelled at the perversity of that ambition which had sought to create a man without considering what a man must suffer to be alone.

***

Morning, when it came, came with a pale and watery sun struggling through clouds yet heavy with rain, and with the sound of wheels upon the wet stones beneath my window. I had not slept; I had watched beside my companion, who at length, overcome by weariness, had sunk into a slumber upon the floor, his head resting against the leg of my table, his breathing deep and regular as that of a child. Mine eyes, red with watching, ached at the unwonted light; my coat was disordered; my papers lay trampled where his foot had inadvertently displaced them. I bethought me, with a sudden pang, of my father, of Elizabeth, of the long silence which my labours had imposed upon my correspondence, and of the reproaches which I must deservedly sustain. While I stood thus divided between present care and distant affection, there came a knock at the outer door of my lodging, followed by a well-remembered voice calling my name with affectionate impatience. It was Henry Clerval, my dearest friend, whose arrival I had indeed been apprised of by letter, but whom, in the agitation of my late pursuits, I had ceased to expect at so early an hour. He had come by the Swiss diligence; his face glowed with health and delight; his portmanteau stood beside the porter; and his eyes sought mine with that open confidence which had ever distinguished him from his youth.

My heart, which had for months been closed to joy, leaped at his sight, and for a moment I forgot the vast sleeper within. I clasped his hand; I inquired after my father, my cousins, Elizabeth; I poured forth questions with a rapidity which must have betrayed my disorder. He answered with his wonted vivacity, yet presently his smile faded, for he remarked my altered visage, my trembling hands, my chamber in disarray. "My dear Frankenstein," said he, "thou art ill; thou hast watched overmuch; thou hast sacrificed thy health to study, as I feared thou wouldst." I endeavoured to laugh, to divert his attention toward his journey, toward Geneva, toward his own permission at last obtained to follow learning rather than merchandize; but my words were incoherent, and my eye wandered continually toward the inner door, which I had closed upon my guest. Clerval, with the quick sympathy of affection, marked my uneasiness and attributed it to surprise; and, with the familiarity of old friendship, he stepped past me toward that door, declaring he would see the den wherein I had immured myself from society.

I would have detained him, but my tongue refused its office; and in another instant the door stood open. The sun, now freed from cloud, poured through my southern window full upon the figure where it sat, awakened by our voices, risen to its full and gigantic height, the borrowed cloak fallen from one shoulder, a crust of bread still grasped in its hand. Henry Clerval recoils from the creature in the narrow sunlit doorway of the Ingolstadt lodging. His countenance, ever so expressive of benevolence and mirth, was transformed in a moment into an image of unmitigated astonishment and abhorrence; he started backward, his hand sought the doorpost for support, his lips parted but emitted no sound. The creature, perceiving this new visitant, advanced a pace with that same outstretched hand which he had offered to me in the night, uttering his plaintive, imperfect murmur, as if he hoped to receive from another human countenance the same forbearance which I had at length accorded. Clerval cried out, I think, though I will not swear to the words, for my blood rushed to my head with a violence that deprived me of distinct hearing; he called upon God, he demanded what devilry was this, he conjured me to explain.

Then was the moment wherein my new resolution was tried as gold is tried in the furnace. Had I fled in the night, I should have left this scene to unfold without a protector for either party; as it was, I stood possessed of a knowledge which both required, and of a duty which neither could comprehend without my aid. Victor Frankenstein steps between Henry Clerval and the creature on the Ingolstadt staircase landing. For Clerval, retreating in his terror, had gained the narrow landing at the head of the stairs, where the balustrade affords but scanty room for two men, much less for two men and such a third; and the creature, distressed by the repulse, had followed with hasty strides, moaning more loudly, while I, recovering my strength through the very extremity of my fear, cast myself into the interval, my back toward my creation, my face toward my friend, my arms extended to maintain that separation which passion threatened to destroy. The posture was perilous; a single thrust from behind would have precipitated me upon Clerval and both of us to the bottom; yet I maintained it, for I perceived that Clerval, in his agitation, had raised the heavy walking-staff which he still carried from his journey, as if to defend himself from an assassin. "Henry! Henry!" I exclaimed, "lower thy weapon, I conjure thee! He means thee no harm! As thou lovest me, restrain thyself!" My voice, sharpened by anguish, seemed at length to penetrate his senses; he paused, though his arm remained uplifted, and gazed upon me as upon one suddenly bereft of reason.

What explanation could I offer which would not consign me to the suspicion of madness, or him to the danger of prosecution as an accomplice in unhallowed arts? I resorted, to my shame, to partial truth, that refuge of those who dare not utter falsehood nor confess entirety. I told him that the being before us was a man afflicted from his birth with a malady which had enlarged his frame and impaired his speech, whom I had taken under my care from motives of charity during my anatomical studies, and whom I had concealed lest the curiosity of the town should render his condition still more wretched. The tale was lame; it halted at every step; Clerval, though generous even to credulity where friendship was concerned, perceived its insufficiency and pressed me with questions which I evaded with an irritability foreign to our intercourse. "Thou art mysterious, Victor," said he, mournfully, "thou concealest from me that which preys upon thy health; hast thou forgotten the compact of our boyhood, that no sorrow of the one should be a secret to the other?" I felt the reproach sink into my soul like a barb; for I loved him tenderly, and the necessity of deceit was among the bitterest fruits of my forbidden labour. Yet what could I disclose? That I had bestowed life upon lifeless matter, that this speechless giant was my workmanship, that the laws of nature, as hitherto understood, were subverted in his person? Such an avowal would have procured me a cell rather than a counsellor. I therefore entreated his patience, his silence, his forbearance toward our unfortunate inmate for but a few days, until I should be recovered sufficiently to arrange our future; and he, with a sigh that reproached me more than anger could have done, promised, though his eye still wandered with dread toward the corner where the creature had withdrawn himself at my command, crouching like a chastised hound.

The day passed in a constraint painful to all three. Clerval, though he endeavoured to resume his cheerful discourse of Geneva and of our mutual friends, started at every movement of our companion, and observed with ill-concealed uneasiness how readily that companion obeyed my slightest gesture, fetching water, replenishing the stove, handling with surprising delicacy the instruments which he had been forbidden to touch. The creature, on his part, seemed to apprehend that he had offended the new-comer, and redoubled his efforts to please; he offered to Clerval a portion of his own bread with an humility that would have moved any heart not preoccupied by terror; and when the offering was declined with averted face, he retired to his corner and fixed his eyes upon the floor with an expression of dejection which I found more insupportable than his former eagerness. I laboured to instruct both at once, to soothe the one without alarming the other; I translated Clerval's animated descriptions of Belrive and Chamounix into the simple nouns which my pupil had begun to comprehend; I intercepted looks, I anticipated misunderstandings; and by evening my temples throbbed with a feverish pain, and my strength was so exhausted that Clerval insisted upon my retiring to rest, offering himself to watch. That offer I could not accept; for who could foresee what might occur in the night between ignorance and fear if the mediator were removed? I therefore feigned a convalescence I did not feel, and prevailed upon him to take my bed while I kept a chair beside the stove, declaring that study had inured me to vigils.

When the house was at last silent, and the clock of the neighbouring church had tolled the hour of midnight, I perceived that concealment within these walls could no longer endure. The porter had already questioned my servant concerning the cries heard upon the stairs; a professor, lodging opposite, had remarked a vast shadow upon my blind; and Clerval himself, though faithful, could not long be expected to harbour a mystery which endangered, as he must suppose, my reputation and my reason. I resolved, therefore, upon a measure as desperate as it was necessary: to remove my charge by night to a more secluded shelter, a small outbuilding belonging to my landlord and used for the storage of faggots, which opened upon the inner court and might be secured with a key. I awakened the creature from his light slumber with a touch upon his shoulder; I placed my finger upon my lips in token of silence, a sign which he already understood; I wrapped him anew in my cloak and in a coarse blanket which I had procured for the purpose; and I led him, with steps as cautious as those of a conspirator, down the back staircase which communicates with the kitchen offices. The moon had set; the rain had ceased; the stones of the court glistened with damp, and our breaths rose visible in the keen air.

Victor Frankenstein leads the creature through the midnight courtyard beneath the Ingolstadt church steeple. How solemn appeared that narrow enclosure at such an hour! On every side rose the dark masses of houses, their windows blind and shuttered; above them, cutting the cloudy heaven, ascended the white steeple of the church, whose clock, just then striking, seemed to number not the hours of ordinary repose but the minutes of my secret guilt. The creature moved beside me with a lightness astonishing in so huge a frame, his bare feet making no sound upon the pavement, his tall figure casting a shadow which mingled with those of the walls. At the gate of the outhouse I paused, key in hand, and looked up into his face, which the faint light from a distant lantern rendered dimly visible; there was in it an expression of trust so absolute, so unquestioning, that I felt my heart contract with a presentiment of the burthen I had assumed. He entered at my bidding without hesitation, and seated himself upon the straw with which the floor was strewn, drawing his covering about him. I spoke to him, low and earnestly, those few words which formed the extent of our common tongue: "Rest. To-morrow. Friend." He repeated the last with painful effort, as if he would engrave it upon his memory; and as I turned the key upon him, not from cruelty but from the necessity of preventing his wandering into peril, that repeated syllable followed me across the court and into my chamber, where Clerval slept unconscious of my absence. I stood long at my window, gazing upon the steeple now shrouded in mist, and knew that I had bound myself henceforth to a path from which neither science nor affection could release me; for I had preserved him from solitude that night, and in so doing had rendered his future, whether for good or for evil, inseparable from my own.
