Alice had hardly settled herself upon the edge of a chair at the large outdoor table, though the Hatter and the March Hare had cried out together that there was not a morsel of room to spare, when she felt something hard and square pressing against her knee through the pocket of her frock; which was odd, for she knew very well what her pockets ought to contain, namely a thimble won at a race, and two crumbs of comfit, and two bits of mushroom, one in each pocket, wrapped most carefully in a scrap of paper, lest they should touch one another and undo her altogether; and besides these there should have been nothing at all, unless a pocket-handkerchief may be counted, which Alice seldom did count, as it was never there when she wanted it.

She slipped her hand in, while the March Hare was pouring tea into the Dormouse's ear by mistake and the Hatter was watching her with his large pale eyes, and she drew out — you may fancy her surprise, and indeed she was not at all sure she was not dreaming it, for Wonderland had already shown her bottles that made her tall and cakes that made her small — a little black pocket telephone, no bigger than a snuff-box, with a round mouth to speak into and a round ear to listen at, and a tiny brass crank at the side, and a bell no bigger than a thimble, which gave, even as she looked, a sharp impatient tremble, as if it were clearing its throat to speak.

Alice sets a little black pocket telephone upon the crowded outdoor tea-table before Hatter and March Hare, and the effect was altogether more instant than any riddle; for the Hatter left off staring at her hair, which he had been upon the point of declaring wanted cutting, and the March Hare left off offering her wine for which there was no bottle, and even the Dormouse, who sat wedged fast between them with his nose in his cup, lifted his head and blinked, as small sleepy animals will when a beetle runs across the table.

"What in the name of Time is that?" said the Hatter, which was more polite than his usual manner, though his voice was quite hoarse with curiosity; and the March Hare cried, "Is it to eat? Is it to drink? Turn it round, let us look at the other side," for he was one of those persons who believe that everything new must either be poured out or cut up, and he stretched his long ears forward over the cups, until one of them dipped in the milk-jug, which nobody wiped, as wiping would have required a clean cloth, and there was no clean cloth to be had.

Alice explained, as well as she could — for she had only seen a telephone once at home, when a cousin who worked at an office had shown her how you turned a handle and asked the young lady at the middle place to join the wires together — that it was a speaking-box, by which two persons ever so far apart might talk as if they stood elbow to elbow; and while she spoke she felt a certain schoolroom pride, such as comes when lessons prove useful after all, though she corrected herself directly, for she was not quite certain whether the middle young lady lived inside the box or outside it, and she did not wish to tell an untruth, particularly to mad people, who are quick to catch you out.

"Pooh!" said the Hatter, tossing his head, so that his tall hat, which was far too large for him, wobbled down over his nose, "we know all about speaking at a distance; Time does it; only Time is cross with me, and will not do it for *me*;" and he looked so injured that Alice was almost sorry for him, till she remembered that he had been extremely rude about her not thinking, and then she was not sorry at all, but only determined to manage the box herself, lest he should spoil it, as he plainly meant to handle it roughly, in the way of little boys with new toys.

Hatter holds the little black telephone to his ear at the crowded outdoor tea-table, with his elbows spread wide among the bread-and-butter, and his hat tipped back, and his eyes shut tight, as if listening hard enough would force the words to come; and indeed there did come a faint humming, like bees shut in a bottle, and then a click, and then a far-off rustle, at which he started so violently that his cup went over, and tea ran in a brown river among the spoons, which nobody mopped, for mopping would have meant moving, and moving would have meant losing one's place, and at a tea-party that never leaves six o'clock a place once lost is never found again.

"It buzzes!" he announced, in the tone of one who confers a favour by noticing a fact, "it buzzes like a Dormouse in a teapot; here, Hare, you have longer ears, do you listen," and before Alice could say *please be careful*, which was upon the very tip of her tongue, he had thrust the glistening ear-piece toward the March Hare, knocking over the sugar-tongs, which fell with a clatter that made the Dormouse murmur in his sleep something about treacle, and sisters, and drawing everything that begins with an M, which was the story he had been trying to tell before Alice came.

March Hare speaks into the little black telephone at the crowded outdoor tea-table, kneeling up upon his chair in his eagerness, with his coat-tails trailing in the butter-dish and his whiskers brushing the mouthpiece, and crying into it, "Hullo! Hullo! Who is there? Is anybody there? Bring us wine! Bring us more tea!" which Alice thought exceedingly ill-bred, for you ought never to shout into a new instrument before you know who keeps the other end, any more than you would shout down a well before you know whether a friend or a dragon lives at the bottom; and she tried to draw it gently away, saying, "You must ask properly, you must give a name, or they cannot join you."

"A name!" said the March Hare, much delighted, for he loved any game with rules he could twist, "then I give the Dormouse! Join us to the Dormouse!" and he laughed until his ears shook, which made Alice quite red with vexation, for she saw that they took the whole matter for a joke, and she, who had begun to hope the box might be of real use — to ask the way to the garden, or to learn whether the mushroom in her pocket was still the right way round — felt her curiosity turning obstinate, which with her was often the beginning of courage.

"If you please," said Alice, in her clearest party voice, the voice she used when reciting before company, though her verses so often went wrong in Wonderland that she hardly liked to raise it, "if this really joins to anywhere, I should like to be joined to the Queen;" for it had come into her head, all at once, that nothing would be so grand, and so decisive, as to ring up royalty itself, and to ask, quite civilly, why the garden door was locked, and whether little girls who drank from proper bottles might walk among the roses without having their heads taken off, which seemed to her a reasonable question, though she doubted very much whether it would be thought so.

At the word *Queen* a most curious change fell upon the table; the Hatter grew suddenly quite pale under the jam upon his cheek, and set down the ear-piece as if it had burned him, and the March Hare tucked his ears flat, as hares will do when dogs are mentioned, and even the Dormouse opened one eye and whispered, "She sang at her concert," which nobody understood, though the Hatter looked as if he understood it only too well, and began brushing crumbs from his coat with great industry, as if brushing could make him invisible.

Alice, who noticed all this, though she pretended to be busy with the crank — for she was learning, you see, to notice and to pretend at once, which is a useful art in company — turned the tiny handle twice, as her cousin had done, and put her mouth close to the round hole, and said, "Please, I want the Queen of Hearts," in the same tone in which at home she would have asked for another slice of bread, only a little firmer, because her heart was beating in a most inconvenient manner against the edge of the table, and she would not for the world have let them see it shake her voice.

For a moment there was only the humming, which grew louder and thinner, like a gnat in a shell, and then a distant thump, and a rattle, as of wooden balls knocked together, and voices crying far away, and the smell, or so Alice fancied, for smells will travel most wonderfully along warm wires, of fresh paint and cut grass and hot pastry; and Alice, with the ear pressed close, could hear, plain as if a door had opened at the end of a long passage, the garden itself, with its fountains hissing, and its soldiers tramping, and a sharp voice counting strokes, which made her think directly of croquet, though she had never in her life played croquet with a live bird for a mallet.

Queen of Hearts lifts a black telephone receiver upon the bright garden croquet-ground, with her crown pushed crooked by haste and her great red gown spread over the furrowed turf, while behind her the gardeners stood upon their ladders with their paint-pots, and the white roses she had ordered to be red showed half-finished, streaked pink and white, like peppermint; and she snatched the instrument, which on her table was no pocket toy but a large black trumpet joined by a cord, as if it had been waiting there for royal use, and set it to her ear with the air of one who expects the whole world to have been kept waiting for her, and not she for the world.

"Who speaks?" came the voice, so loud through the little box that the Hatter jumped, and the March Hare upset the milk, and the Dormouse woke entirely, "who dares to ring when I am at my game? Speak at once, or I will have your head!" which was uttered with such practiced ease that Alice understood directly this was a person accustomed to settling every difficulty, from overdone tarts to crooked croquet-hoops, by the same short remedy; and though her knees trembled under the tablecloth, where nobody could see them, she resolved not to be frightened before she had said her say, for fright, as she told herself severely, is no excuse for bad manners.

Alice speaks into the little telephone at the crowded outdoor tea-table before Hatter and March Hare, sitting very upright with her hands folded round the box to keep them steady, while the Hatter crouched behind a pile of dirty cups as if he hoped the wire would not carry his face as well as his voice, and the March Hare leaned so close that his whiskers tickled her ear, and whispered, "Ask her the riddle! Ask her why a raven is like a writing-desk!" which Alice had not the least intention of doing, for she wanted no more riddles, having had quite enough of unanswered ones for one afternoon.

"If you please, Majesty," said Alice, and she was pleased to find her *please* came out quite round and distinct, "I am a little girl at tea, and I only wished to know whether I might come into your beautiful garden by the little door, for I have got the golden key quite safe, and I am *quite* civil, and I do not paint roses wrong, indeed I do not;" and then, because the humming seemed to grow impatient, she added, in a smaller voice, "and the Hatter sends his respects, I think;" which was not strictly true, for the Hatter was at that moment shaking his head violently behind the teapot and making dreadful faces to stop her, but Alice thought it kinder to include him, as he looked so frightened, though kindness, as she was to learn, is not always wise with queens.

"The Hatter!" cried the far voice, sharpening at once, as a knife sharpens upon stone, "the Hatter who murdered Time at my concert? The wretch who sang twinkle-twinkle out of tune and spoiled my soup? Hold him! Keep him there! I will send my soldiers! His head shall be taken this very evening!" and there followed a great clatter, as if a mallet had been thrown down upon stone, and a shouting of cards running, and the gardeners dropping their brushes, all of which Alice heard with growing horror, for she had meant to make peace, and instead she had brought war, like a messenger-pigeon that carries a hawk upon its back.

"Oh! I did not mean —" began Alice, but the box only buzzed, for the Queen was now speaking to someone else at her end, giving orders thick and fast about shutting gates and sharpening axes and finding the white rabbit to write them down, which made Alice feel exceedingly guilty, as if she had rung a fire-bell for fun; and she looked reproachfully at the March Hare, who had begun to giggle in a nervous manner, and at the Hatter, who had turned the colour of cold tea, and who kept whispering, "You have done it! You have told her where we are! She never knew we were here till you rang!" which was unjust, as Alice pointed out, for the Queen had invited everyone to croquet, though perhaps, she admitted to herself, an invitation is not the same as an address.

"Nonsense!" said Alice at last, aloud, though whether to herself or to the Queen or to the trembling gentlemen before her she hardly knew, "it is only a speaking-box; she cannot come through the wire, you know;" but even as she said it she was not quite sure, for in Wonderland bottles bring bigness and pebbles turn to cakes, and why should not a queen come travelling along a wire, growing smaller and smaller to get through, and then swelling to full size in the milk-jug? The thought made her draw her hands back from the box, lest a royal hand should seize her fingers, which the March Hare perceived, and laughed outright, though his laugh cracked in the middle.

"You must un-ring her!" hissed the Hatter, forgetting all his rudeness in terror, "tell her we are gone! Tell her it was the Dormouse! Tell her it was Time!" and he seized the tablecloth with both hands, as if to pull it over his head, which only dragged half the tea-things toward him, and set the Dormouse rolling among the spoons, where he sat up, very tousled and indignant, and said, "I was dreaming of treacle, and you have spoiled it with shouting," which under other circumstances would have made Alice laugh, but now only made her feel how late it was getting, and how tangled everything had grown, like wool after a kitten has played with it.

Alice pressed the ear-piece tighter, for she felt responsible, as the person who had turned the handle must see the kettle through to boiling, and she said, very loudly and distinctly, "Your Majesty, please do not send anyone; we are only having tea, and there is no room, and the Hatter is very sorry about Time, are you not?" and she looked hard at the Hatter, to make him nod, which he did, after a fashion, though his nod shook his hat over his eyes, so that he looked sorrier than he perhaps was; and the March Hare added, in a shrill whisper that carried straight into the mouthpiece, "And the butter was the very best!" which Alice could have boxed his ears for, as it explained nothing and recalled everything.

"Sorry?" repeated the Queen, and Alice could hear the smile without seeing it, which is a horrid kind of smile to hear, "we shall see how sorry when his head is off his shoulders! Keep him till we come! And as for you, child, who rings queens up as if they were fishmongers, you shall be my witness! Come to my court at once, or I will fetch you!" and the wire sang with the slam of her trumpet hung up, leaving only the bees-in-a-bottle hum, which presently died also, as if the garden had shut its gate with a bang, though far away Alice fancied she still heard marching feet upon gravel, which might have been only her own heart thumping in her ears.

Hatter scatters teacups across the crowded outdoor tea-table before Alice and March Hare, springing to his feet with his coat flying and his hat falling, and sweeping his arm wide among the cups and saucers, so that they leapt and spun and poured their cold tea in arcs over the cloth, while the bread-and-butter slid to the edge and the Dormouse clutched at a spoon to keep from being swept away himself; and Alice sprang back, clutching the little black box, which now only hummed faintly, like a fly tired of buzzing, while the March Hare caught at the Hatter's sleeve, crying, "Not that way! The soldiers come this way!" though how he knew which way soldiers come along a telephone wire Alice could not conceive.

"You see!" panted the Hatter, with his pale face now flushed to the ears, and his eyes wild as if Time himself were after him, "this is what comes of thinking and ringing! I told you Time would not mend! Now we must all change places! Change places, all of you!" and he began dragging chairs about with tremendous clatter, though there was nowhere to change to, except among the spilt tea and the broken crusts, which made the whole proceeding more ridiculous than dreadful, except that his hands shook so piteously that Alice felt her anger melting, as butter melts when you are not watching it, into something very like pity.

Alice stood with the silent box in her hand, the brass crank still warm from her turning, and looked from the ruined tea to the wood-path that led, as the Cheshire Cat had grinned to her, toward the March Hare's house and beyond it to the garden wall; and she understood, with a sinking clearness, that by seeking the shortest way — a word through the air instead of a walk upon her feet — she had shortened nothing, but had given the Queen both her name and her company, and had set the soldiers marching before their time; which was a dear price to pay for curiosity, though curiosity, as she reminded herself, tucking a loose lock behind her ear, was the very thing that had brought the box into her pocket at all, and would, she feared, make her follow the path to see what came of it.

The March Hare, who had recovered his spirits with surprising quickness, as persons do whose fright is chiefly for others, was already wiping a cup with his coat-tail and offering it to her, saying, "Have some more tea? Though there is none left, which makes it very easy to pour;" and the Dormouse, having crawled into the teapot for safety, poked his nose out and murmured, "Ring them again, miss, and ask for treacle," which made Alice laugh in spite of herself, a short breathless laugh that did not quite steady her; and the Hatter, with his hat over one eye and his watch, smeared with butter, held tight in his hand, stood listening down the path, as if he already heard boots among the leaves, and beckoned to her, urgent and mute, to come and hide before the court should find them all at tea.

remixes.chapter:
The clock of the high white church had long since told the first hour after midnight, and still I laboured among the vessels and irons of my solitary chamber above the gallery, while the rain beat without ceasing upon the glass and the candle sank low in its socket and threw an uncertain glimmer upon the boards. For months I had denied myself society and air and needful rest, that I might complete the frame which lay extended at my feet, and on that wet November night the last connexion was finished and nothing remained but to commit the trial which my soul at once desired and dreaded. With hands that shook from watching and from expectation, I applied the instruments of life around the motionless head and breast, and held my own breath as the power I had summoned with such labour passed into the lifeless organisation.

A shudder ran through the great limbs, the broad breast heaved with a hard and difficult respiration, and beneath lids that had seemed sealed for ever a dull and yellowish eye unclosed and fixed itself upon the light. O miserable triumph of my art! I had chosen each portion with a vain hope of beauty, and had proportioned the stature to near eight feet that the minuteness of the parts might be less difficult to manage; yet the sallow skin, drawn too tightly over the dark lines of muscle and of artery, the long black hair flowing over the shoulders, the white and even teeth set in straight and bloodless lips, served only to render more dreadful the watery orbs that gazed from their pale and shrivelled sockets. Where I had dreamed of grace, there lived only a vast and yellow visage, convulsed into motion, and terrible to behold.

All that ardour with which I had pursued my undertaking fell from me in a single instant, as a cloak falls from the shoulders of a traveller overtaken by storm, and left me naked to loathing and to affright. I had desired the accomplishment of my toils with a fervour beyond all moderation; I had sacrificed health and correspondence and the communion of my friends to this one purpose; and now that the purpose breathed, the dream lost its fairness and became a torment. Unable to sustain the aspect of the being I had animated, I hurried from the workshop into my bed-chamber and paced the narrow floor in distraction, now starting at the creak of a board, now rebuking my own folly, yet daring neither to return nor to extinguish the light that burned behind the door.

At length weariness overcame tumult, and I cast myself in my clothes upon the bed and sought a brief oblivion which presently assumed the form of tormenting visions. Methought Elizabeth, in the bloom of her health and with her bright hair uncovered, walked toward me through the streets of this foreign town, and I hastened to embrace her with delight; but when my lips touched her cheek, her countenance altered and grew cold and livid, and I found that I enfolded in my arms the lifeless form of my mother, wrapped in flannel for the grave, while creeping things moved in the folds of the cloth. I awoke with a cry, my forehead damp, my teeth striking together, and every joint trembling, as if a fever had seized me in the night.

Through the chinks of the shutters the moon, obscured by driving cloud, cast a wan and yellow beam across the curtains, and by that beam I perceived, standing close beside me, the figure I had left extended in the chamber above. He had lifted the curtain with one immense hand, and his eyes were bent steadfastly upon my face; his jaws parted and gave forth a low and broken murmur without words, and the muscles of his cheeks drew upward into what in a human countenance would have been a smile. One hand was advanced toward me, not in menace, as my distempered fancy first conceived, but with a slow and uncertain motion, as a child extends its arm to detain the parent who would leave it.

I did not fly.

My limbs had already gathered themselves for the stairs, and my heart counselled the courtyard below and the long watches of the night spent in pacing to and fro with listening ears; yet I remained upon the edge of the mattress, held less by courage than by a sudden and piercing sense of my own baseness. He whom I had deserted within the first hour of his breath stood seeking me in the dark, and his vast fingers trembled in the air. I put forth my own thin hand, cold with sweat, and clasped his; the palm that enclosed mine was warm and damp as with new life, the bones large as those of no common man, the skin yielding and strange to the touch. The pressure answered mine with a gentle and enquiring force, and the low sounds ceased, as if attention had absorbed him. O wretchedness and wonder together! That I, who had fled from my own work as from a crime, should feel it learn comfort from my touch.

Learn from me, my friend, if any lesson may be drawn from that hour of loathing conquered less by virtue than by shame; for who shall bestow existence and then refuse the least offices of humanity to the thing he has called forth? I had sought to be as a creator, and had imagined gratitude and benediction; I had not imagined this mute appeal, more powerful than eloquence. What had I expected, that a new-born soul, if soul it were, should at once comprehend solitude and ask nothing? The rain still murmured upon the panes, the candle in the farther room guttered toward extinction, and I sat with my hand in that mighty grasp, while horror by slow degrees gave place to a piteous and reluctant duty.

He was naked except for some coarse covering I had thrown across his loins during my labour, and he shivered in the chill that entered by the ill-closed shutters; his breath came short, and his eyes wandered from my face to the dying fire and back again with the helpless curiosity of infancy. I rose, still retaining his fingers with my left hand lest he should conceive himself forsaken, and with my right poured water from the ewer into a cup and held it to his lips. He drank with difficulty, spilling much upon his breast, and then uttered a soft noise that was neither speech nor moan, but seemed content. I drew the woollen coverlet from my own bed and cast it about his shoulders; he gathered it close with an awkward haste, and looked toward me again, as if to learn whether this kindness would continue.

Lest any footstep in the house should discover us, I led him, step by uncertain step, up the narrow stair into the workshop, where the instruments lay scattered and the oil lamp still burned above the table. The place smelt of spirits and of heated metal, and the rain drummed louder beneath the roof. Upon a shelf stood the remains of my evening meal, a loaf and cheese untouched in my absorption. I broke the bread and softened a morsel in water, for his teeth, though perfect, worked without skill, and I feared he might choke. I knelt upon the cold boards with the food in my hands, that my stature might be less removed from his as he sat huddled upon the low stool I had used for my watches, the coverlet trailing about his enormous limbs, the lamplight falling upon his dark hair and yellow brow. He took the bread eagerly yet without violence, and ate while his eyes remained fixed upon my countenance, as a dog watches the hand that feeds it and seeks in the face the promise of more.

Through that long night I taught him, if teaching it may be called, the smallest necessities of the body; to drink without spilling, to remain seated when I raised my palm, to draw the blanket closer when the wind sighed through the casement. Each success filled me with a strange and melancholy exultation, such as a father might feel who beholds his child surmount a fever, dashed instantly by the remembrance of what eyes regarded me and what whispers would arise in Ingolstadt if this commerce were known. My candle burned out and I lit another; my limbs ached for want of sleep, and a dull pain settled behind my eyes. Yet I barred the workshop door and placed a chest against it, for the porter passed early upon his rounds, and the servant who brought my breakfast must not find this guest. *Mine*, I thought, with a pang that partook of both fondness and despair; he is *mine*, and none other will own him.

***

Morning came dismal and wet, the white steeple shewing indistinct through mist, the clock pointing to the sixth hour, when I ventured with trembling caution into the street to breathe and to consider. The rain had lessened to a thin drizzle, the stones shone darkly, and the gates of the court stood open. Scarce had I reached the corner by the inn where the diligences discharge their passengers, when a Swiss coach drew up amid splashing wheels, the door was flung open, and a well-known voice called my name with delight. It was Henry Clerval, arrived without warning, his face bright with travel and affection, his cloak damp, his portmanteau already in the ostler’s hand. He sprung down and seized both my hands, surveying me with joy that swiftly altered into concern at my thinness and pallor.

"My dearest Victor, at last I behold you," he cried, retaining my hands and searching my features, "and yet how altered you appear, as if study had consumed you like a wasting illness. Your father and Elizabeth charged me with a thousand remembrances, and complained, though with love, of your long silence; I promised to render an exact account of your health and spirits, and to bring you back, if not in person, at least in faithful description. Tell me, then, how you have lived, and why your eyes are so wild, and whether Ingolstadt has treated you kindly, for I will not be satisfied with evasions." His warmth pierced me, for I had no reply that was not a falsehood or a confession that must appal him, and I stammered some excuse of excessive labour now happily concluded, and drew him hastily toward my college, fearing each instant lest a cry from my barred chamber should betray me.

We mounted the familiar stair, Henry discoursing of Geneva and of his hopes of learning, while I grew colder with every step. At the door of my lodging I attempted to turn him toward the lower parlour, alleging the disorder of my rooms after a night of study; but he laughed and pressed forward with the freedom of old friendship, and perceived at once the barred door of the upper workshop and the chest thrust against it. His gaiety paused; he set himself directly in my path and prevented my hand from reaching the lock, demanding with affectionate obstinacy what mystery I concealed and whether illness or debt or some unhappy entanglement had made me thus secretive. The rain beat upon the roof above us, a drop fell from his cloak upon the boards, and I stood with my back to that forbidden door, feeling the beating of my own arteries and the weight of the knowledge behind me.

At that moment a sound issued from within, a heavy shifting of weight and a low inarticulate murmur, such as I had heard in the night, followed by a soft knocking, as of a large hand essaying the panels. Henry started and grew pale, then coloured with a sudden resolution. "Victor," said he in a lowered voice, "there is some living thing within. You are ill, my friend, and perhaps deluded; suffer me to enter with you, for whatever it may be, you shall not face it alone." I entreated, I commanded, I invoked our childhood; all was vain against his devoted fear for me. With shaking fingers I drew aside the chest and turned the key, resolved that if ruin must come, it should come through truth rather than through longer deceit.

The lamp still burned low upon the table, and in its circle, wrapped in my coverlet, sat the being I had animated, now risen at our entrance and sunk again upon his knees with his vast hands extended in supplication. The light fell upon his yellow brow and flowing black hair, upon his broad breast heaving with agitation, upon those watery eyes fixed not upon me but upon the stranger with an expression of timid hope. Henry recoiled to the wall of the narrow lodging, his hand seeking the doorpost, his lips parted, deprived for an instant of speech by the sudden apparition. The creature uttered no threat; he remained kneeling, his head bent, his palms open and empty, as I had taught him in the night to ask for bread, now asking, though he knew it not, for forbearance.

"God preserve us!" exclaimed Henry at last, his voice hoarse and scarcely his own. "Victor, what is this? What devilry have you practised in this chamber? Speak, I conjure you, for my senses reel. Is this a man afflicted with disease, or some mockery of our nature contrived by your philosophy?" He would have cried out for the porter, would have fled down the stairs to summon aid, so violent was the conflict in his generous breast between terror and loyalty. I seized his arm, not roughly, but with the desperation of one who sees all he loves suspended over an abyss, and besought him in broken sentences to master his alarm and hear me before he condemned either my work or me.

I cast myself into the narrow opening of the upper doorway, with one arm extended toward Henry and the other toward the kneeling figure, barring all passage between them. "Stay, Henry, I implore you, by our earliest friendship and by all that is holy in affection!" I cried. "This being lives by my act, however unlawful that act may have been; he has harmed no one, he knows neither speech nor evil, and his only crime is the hideousness which my own hands bestowed. If you raise the town upon us, they will destroy him as a monster and me as a sorcerer, and my father and Elizabeth will learn my infamy together with my death. Grant me but a little time, and I will remove him where no eye shall behold him, and will answer to Heaven and to you for what I have done." My voice failed, my knees trembled, yet I did not quit my post; behind me the creature remained motionless, as if comprehending that his fate hung upon my words.

Henry regarded me long, his breast labouring, his countenance passing from horror to pity and to a deep and wounded reproach. He was, as ever, humane beyond common men, quick to succour distress, yet no enthusiast who could lightly pardon a sacrilege against nature. "You ask much, Victor," he said at last, slowly, "more than a friend should be required to grant. You have evidently suffered and erred greatly, and I fear your reason has been shaken by solitude. Yet I cannot deliver you to ruin upon a single view. I will keep silence until to-morrow night, and will aid you to conceal this unfortunate, on condition that you promise to disclose to me the whole of your proceedings and to seek no further in these forbidden arts." The concession cost him dear; I saw it in his averted eyes and in the coldness of his hand when I pressed it in gratitude. The frank confidence of our boyhood had received its first wound.

That wound I must deepen before it could heal, for no lodging in the town could long conceal so vast an inmate. When darkness fell and the rain renewed its dismal patter upon the stones, I wrapped him in a coarse cloak procured from a Jew dealer near the bridge, drawing the hood low over his brow and hair, and charged Henry to watch the stair and warn me with a cough should any person approach. Then, with my arm linked through his that I might guide his uncertain steps and restrain him should fear overtake him, I conducted him down the back stair and through the empty stone court toward a ruinous woodshed without the college wall which I had marked in former walks. The porter dozed by his lodge fire, the yard lay black and gleaming with wet, and our shadows moved together across the puddles, his gigantic, mine slight beside him. He obeyed each pressure of my hand, and uttered no sound louder than his laboured breath.

Within the shed, amid faggots and the smell of damp bark, I spread dry straw and set bread and water beside him, and by signs bade him remain. He clasped my hand once more with that gentle force I had first felt beside my bed, and then released it. As I barred the crazy door and turned toward the lights of my lodging, where Henry awaited me with questions I dreaded to answer, I understood that I had not avoided ruin by my forbearance; I had only chosen another ruin, slower and more secret, in which another life now depended wholly upon my constancy.

The tea-table stood all askew in the late afternoon sunshine, with its long white cloth stained in great brown rings and littered from end to end with cups and saucers and crumbs of bread-and-butter, and the March Hare and the Hatter sat squeezed together at one corner with their elbows among the jam-pots, while the Dormouse dozed with his nose in a saucer between them and breathed in a slow, teaboard sort of way that lifted a teaspoon whenever he sighed. Alice had taken the only chair that was in any degree free from marmalade, and her shoes, which had grown very tight with walking through roots and damp grass, pinched her toes under the table, and a loose lock of her hair would keep falling forward into her eyes, so that she was obliged every minute to toss her head back, which is a difficult thing to do politely when one is trying to look dignified. The Hatter had just told her, in that blunt, private sort of manner he used for remarks about other people's faces and tempers, that she had no business to open her mouth at all unless she had first turned her thoughts quite inside out to see if there was anything worth showing; and Alice felt her cheeks grow hot, for she *had* been thinking, very hard indeed, about riddles without answers and watches that told the day of the month but not the hour, which seemed to her quite as much thinking as any tea-table had a right to expect.

She might, you will observe, have got up and walked away in a pet, as any child with proper spirit might have done after being lectured upon thinking by a person who lived perpetually at six o'clock and buttered his own watch; but there was something in the waste and clatter of that endless tea that made her unwilling to be beaten by it, and something besides, a small, obstinate curiosity, which said that if great people could be rude with impunity there must be some greater person to appeal to, and that she, Alice, knew exactly where to find one. For in the pocket of her frock, wrapped in a scrap of paper beside the two crumbs of mushroom, the right-hand crumb and the left-hand crumb, that she kept for growing taller or shorter as occasion required, there lay a thing she had carried about all that sultry day without once remembering it, because in Wonderland one so seldom has leisure to remember what one has in one's pockets.

It was a pocket telephone, no larger than a comfit-box, made of black japanned tin with a brass crank at the side and a round ear-piece no bigger than a shilling joined to it by a cord twisted like a pig's tail, which sprang back when pulled and hummed faintly when shaken, as if there were bees shut up inside it. Alice had brought it from home for playing at exchanges with her sister, where one person was to be the office and say "Who do you require?" in a deep voice, and she had quite forgotten it through falling down wells and swimming in salt water and being nursed by a Duchess; but the feel of the cold crank against her knuckles brought it all back, and she thought, with that sudden clearness which sometimes comes in the midst of nonsense, that if the wire ran nowhere in particular, which in this place seemed very likely, it might for that very reason run *everywhere*, and most particularly to a palace.

"If you please," said Alice, with great politeness, for she always began politely even when she meant to be very firm afterwards, "I have a pocket telephone, and I mean to consult a person of authority about manners at tea."

The Hatter stared at her over his great cup, with his pale eyes very wide, and the March Hare pricked up his long ears until the sun shone pink through the tips of them, and both of them laughed in that unpleasant, knowledgeable way people laugh when they believe they have caught another person in ignorance of wires and poles.

"A telephone without a wire!" cried the Hatter, pointing his teaspoon at her as if it were a finger. "Why, you might as well try to drink tea without a cup. Where is your post, pray, and where is your shilling for the office?"

"There is no office," said the March Hare, pouring more tea into his own saucer to show how little he cared, "and there is no wire, and if there were, there would be nobody at the other end but ourselves, which would be a great waste of politeness."

Alice said nothing in reply to this, which was perhaps the most dignified thing she had done all afternoon, but she set her little black box upright upon the cloth among the spoons, where the sun caught the brass and made it wink, and she held it up that they might both see it plainly. Alice holds a small black pocket telephone before Hatter and March Hare at the tea-table, lifting it high above the slop and the crumbs, with the cord dangling and the crank glittering, while the Hatter leaned forward with his mouth open and the March Hare stopped with his jug tilted in mid-air, and even the Dormouse opened one eye to look at the shining thing before he sneezed and shut it again. It was a proper exhibition, and Alice took her time over it, turning the crank slowly twice round to show that it worked, for she felt that if one is to be told one does not think, the best answer is to do something very deliberate indeed.

The crank gave a brisk, whirring click, and then a low, distant humming began inside the box, like a fly trapped in a thimble, growing louder and thinner by turns, as humming does when it comes through a long distance. The Hatter put his hands over his ears in pretence of pain, and the March Hare cried out that she had wound up a wasp, but Alice, who knew the sound of an exchange very well from play, held up her finger for silence, which only made the Hatter grin the more, and waited with her head a little on one side, listening.

"Exchange!" said Alice clearly into the mouth-hole, feeling very business-like and grown-up. "I require the Queen of Hearts, if you please."

There was a series of sharp clicks, as of knitting-needles dropped upon a floor, and then a pause in which Alice could hear her own breathing and the heavy ticking of the Hatter's watch, which lay among the cups with butter glistening upon its works, and then, quite suddenly and very close, a hard, short voice spoke in the ear-piece, a voice accustomed to giving orders before asking questions.

Alice presses the telephone receiver to her ear before Hatter and March Hare at the tea-table, with her elbow planted firmly upon the cloth to keep the box steady and her hair falling across her cheek as she bends, while the Hatter watches her with his teacup half-way to his lips and the March Hare crouches with both paws upon the table edge, and the whole litter of cups and plates seems to lean toward that one small black circle from which a voice, thin and angry and entirely certain of itself, is pouring like tea from a pot. Alice's eyes grew larger as she listened, for the voice said, "Who presumes to ring? Speak at once and do not simper," in a tone that made the cord itself seem to stiffen, and Alice knew, with a flutter under her pinafore that was half delight and half fright, that she had indeed got through to somebody quite royal and quite awake.

"If you please, your Majesty," said Alice, and she tried to curtsey sitting down, which is an awkward business and caused her to knock her knee against the table-leg, "I am Alice, and I am at a tea-table where there is no room though there is plenty of room, and they ask riddles without answers and quarrel about time, and I thought you, who understand rules, would tell me whether it is manners to find fault with a guest who has only just sat down."

"A guest!" said the voice in the telephone, so sharp that Alice held the receiver a little farther off. "What guest? What table? What riddle? Answer in order and leave out the sighs."

Now this was very like a lesson, and Alice, who was used to lessons, drew a long breath and began to explain about the table under the tree and the house with chimneys like ears and the watch in the teapot of conversation, if one might call it so, and as she spoke the Hatter's face changed by degrees from pink to white and from white to a sort of damp grey, like paper left out in rain. He knew that voice; indeed how could he help knowing it, for it was the same voice that had pronounced his singing to be murder and his time to be forfeit, after which Time himself, as he had often declared to the Hare over their cold tea, had refused to do another stroke of work for him or to move past six o'clock by so much as a crumb. He plucked at his coat, which was too large for his thin shoulders, and whispered hoarsely to the March Hare, "It is *her*!" and the March Hare whispered back, "Hush!" though neither of them had been speaking aloud enough for Alice to have noticed if she had not been so quick at noticing whispers.

"And who is there with you, child?" demanded the Queen through the humming wire, for queens in all countries have a particular knack for hearing whispers through doors and floors and telephone boxes. "Mention their names and do not stammer."

"There is a Hatter and a March Hare," said Alice obligingly, "and a Dormouse asleep, and a great many cups."

At the word Hatter there came such a silence upon the wire that Alice thought the connection had broken, and then a sound that was neither humming nor clicking but more like the scratching of a large pen, as if somebody at the other end were drawing a line under a name in a book.

Before Alice could ask whether she was still required, the Hatter, with a suddenness that upset three cups and sent a spoon spinning into the sugar-basin, thrust his long, thin hand across the table and seized the receiver from her, crying that a private instrument must not be monopolised and that he, as master of the table, had a right to explain. Hatter speaks into the telephone receiver beside Alice and March Hare at the tea-table, standing half up with his coat-tails in the butter-dish and his tall hat tipped over one eye, with the black mouth-piece jammed against his mouth and his other hand clutching Alice's sleeve to keep himself steady, while Alice sits back with her hands in her lap and her mouth pursed in surprise and the March Hare peers round the Hatter's elbow with his whiskers quivering. He spoke very fast and very loud, as frightened people do when they hope that loudness will pass for cheerfulness, saying, "Your Majesty will graciously recall that it was only a song, and a very short song, and the butter in the works was entirely the Hare's best butter and not mine," and much more to the same effect, tumbling his words over one another until the wire buzzed with them.

"Sing!" said the Queen, and though Alice could now only catch fragments, for the receiver was pressed to the Hatter's ear, that one word came through clear and terrible. "Sing, indeed! Are you the little man who murdered my time at the concert and left my evenings without an evening? Do not move from that table. Do not drink another cup. I am coming myself to see your head."

The March Hare, who had been listening with his ears laid flat, as hares do when rain is coming, gave a great start at this, for he had no desire to have his own ears examined by royalty in connection with butter and watches, and with the air of a person who has thought of a very clever expedient he seized the teapot, which was large and brown and dripping from the spout, and lifted it high with both paws. March Hare pours tea over the pocket telephone before Alice at the crowded tea-table, tilting the fat brown pot until a thick amber stream falls hissing upon the black japanned lid and runs in rivulets down the brass crank and into the mouth-hole, while Alice springs back with her hands thrown up and her frock spotted and the Hatter shouts and tries to shelter the receiver under his hat and the cups rattle with the jar. It was done in an instant and with great thoroughness, as if drowning the box could drown the voice inside it, and for a moment the humming rose to a choking gurgle and then sank into a wet, sputtering silence, broken only by the drip of tea from the table edge upon Alice's shoes.

"There!" said the March Hare triumphantly, setting down the empty pot. "No box, no voice. You cannot hang a drowned telephone."

"You have spoilt my instrument," said Alice, very angry indeed, for the box was her own property and the tea was running into the paper that held her mushroom crumbs and making them soggy, "and you have spoilt your own manners into the bargain, which is a great deal worse, though I daresay you will not think so."

"Hush!" whispered the Hatter, who was still holding the dead receiver to his ear as if he hoped to hear forgiveness leaking out of it. "Do you not hear wheels? Do you not hear feet? She said she was coming, and in this place coming is often the same as come."

Indeed there was a new sound beyond the garden fence, a heavy, rhythmic trampling intermingled with the jingling of harness and the sharp tapping of a stick upon gravel, growing louder with every breath, and the bees that had been humming about the jam suddenly rose in a cloud and fled, and the sunlight seemed to grow hotter upon Alice's neck. The Dormouse woke with a squeak and dived under the tablecloth, and the March Hare began hastily to turn all the cups upside down, as if an orderly table might excuse a disorderly conscience, and the Hatter tried to look small behind his own hat, which is difficult when the hat is taller than the man.

Round the corner of the house with the fur-thatched roof there swept a procession, though a very small one for such a noise, headed by a stout, square-shouldered woman in a voluminous gown patterned all over with red hearts, with a golden crown set straight upon her dark hair and her arms folded tight across her chest, and behind her two card soldiers shuffling their flat feet and carrying a rope between them as if they already knew what it was for. Her face, which was broad and commanding, was flushed a deep, mottled crimson with walking fast in the heat, and her eyes fixed at once upon the tea-table and upon the wet black box steaming faintly in the sun.

"Which is the singer?" said the Queen of Hearts, without any form of greeting, for she held that greeting wasted time which might be better spent in sentencing. "Point him out and do not tell lies, for I have his voice still buzzing in my ear."

The March Hare pointed at once at the Hatter, and the Hatter pointed at once at the March Hare, and both pointed so eagerly that their fingers nearly crossed, and Alice, who felt that truth was getting very little attention, said plainly, "He sang at your concert, but it was long ago, and he has had nothing but tea since, which seems to me punishment enough for most songs."

The Queen paid no more heed to this sensible observation than if a spoon had spoken, but stepped straight up to the trembling host, her wide skirts brushing the cups from the table edge with a crash that made the Dormouse moan under the cloth, and seized him with a firm, practised grasp. Queen of Hearts seizes Hatter by the collar before Alice at the crowded tea-table, with her stout right hand twisted tight in his spotted cravat and her left hand planted upon her hip and her crown nodding forward with the effort, while the Hatter stands on tiptoe with his chin forced up and his pale face blotched and his tall hat toppling, and Alice rises from her chair with her hands outstretched and her hair across her eyes and the March Hare shrinks back with the empty teapot held before him like a shield. It was a dreadful and very particular tableau, the tea dripping and the cards rustling and the sun beating down upon brass and china, and Alice felt, with a sudden coldness quite different from curiosity, that ringing for justice and getting it were two things as unlike as a riddle and its answer.

"You shall sing no more treason at my tables," said the Queen, shaking him a little with each word, so that his teeth clicked. "Tie his hands and keep his mouth for the trial. And for this wet mischief," she added, kicking the ruined telephone with the toe of her slipper until it spun among the saucers, "somebody shall pay in saucers."

"It was the Hare's butter and the Hare's tea!" cried the Hatter faintly. "I am a poor man and I only keep tea!"

"You keep very bad company," said the Queen, "which is the same thing. March!"

The soldiers shuffled forward, and the March Hare, seeing the rope, dropped the teapot with a clatter and bolted behind Alice's chair, breathing fast through his nose upon her neck, which was exceedingly unpleasant, while the Dormouse, feeling himself deserted, crept out and attempted to get into the teapot for safety, as he had been taught to do upon emergencies. Alice, who had rung the bell and now found the house on fire, as persons who meddle with royalty very often do, looked from the ruined box, which had been her own and now lay drowned and silent, to the Hatter's imploring eyes, and understood, with a clearness that made her ashamed of her former cleverness, that she had paid for her vindication with somebody else's liberty, and at a very dear rate.

She had still, thank goodness, the mushroom crumbs in their soggy paper, though whether they would still work after a bath of tea she could not tell, and she had still her own legs, which, though short, were very good at running when there was no time for thinking. The little door in the trunk of the great tree stood ajar behind the table, showing darkness within and a faint gleam as of lamps far off, and while the Queen was occupied in directing the soldiers to tie a proper knot, which they, being cards, performed very clumsily, Alice gathered her skirts in her hands. Alice hurries through the little tree door beside March Hare at the crowded tea-table, darting low beneath the hanging boughs with her frock caught back and her shoes flashing upon the roots, while the March Hare stands beside the table with one paw still stretched toward her and his long ears thrown back with alarm and the overturned cups gleaming behind him. She did not look back to see whether he meant to follow or to betray, but slipped sideways through the narrow opening, bark scraping her elbows, into the cool, hollow dark where the hum of bees and the clink of china died all at once, as humming always does when one passes through wood.

***

The passage was short and smelt of damp earth and old cupboards, and it opened, as passages in dreams will, without any staircase worth mentioning, into the long, low hall with its lamps burning in a row and its doors shut all round like so many watching eyes. The three-legged glass table stood in the middle quite as she had left it, ages ago, with the tiny golden key lying upon it winking in the lamplight, and the little curtain that hid the fifteen-inch door hung dusty and still. Alice leaned against the cold wall with her heart thumping against her ribs and her spotted frock clinging to her knees, listening to the muffled shouting that came, very faint and thin, through the bark of the tree, as if a queen might still be giving orders on the other side of wood, and she pressed the damp paper of mushroom crumbs tight in her fist. She had got her knowledge of Time and her proof about thinking, and she had lost her telephone and very nearly her appetite for justice; and what she should do next, whether to nibble right or left, or whether to unlock the garden door at all while the gardener's mistress was in such a temper, was a question she had no leisure, just at present, to decide.
